papers.title: Simulation-based inference for gravitational-wave cosmology: parameter reconstruction of a first-order electroweak phase transition
papers.authors: Thomas Biekötter, Andrii Dashko, Kateryna Radchenko
papers.abstract: The detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) from a cosmological first- order phase transition would be unambiguous evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model, with a strong electroweak phase transition (EWPT) at LISA as a prime example. Reconstructing the underlying model from such a signal is challenging, since the map from the model parameters to the spectrum is degenerate and strong transitions occupy only small and sparse regions of parameter space. We show that simulation-based inference (SBI), a likelihood-free approach applicable to generic SGWB sources, provides a reliable parameter reconstruction despite these difficulties. We first apply SBI to the thermodynamic parameters characterizing the transition, namely its strength, inverse duration, temperature and bubble wall velocity. As a concrete application, we then consider a strong EWPT in a singlet extension of the Standard Model and reconstruct the model parameters from the resulting SGWB. We find that the SBI posteriors agree with those of a likelihood-based Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis, at negligible cost per data set once the network has been trained. Using the network posterior as the proposal for importance sampling with the exact likelihood further corrects its remaining deviations, at a sampling efficiency several orders of magnitude higher than sampling from the prior. SBI thus offers a fast and flexible framework for the cosmological science case of LISA

conclusions: Neural posterior estimation (NPE) accurately recovers both thermodynamic transition parameters ($T_n, \alpha, \beta/H_*, v_w$) and fundamental cxSM particle parameters ($m_S, \lambda_S, \lambda_{HS}$) in good agreement with full MCMC runs, returning posteriors for a new spectrum in ~1 second once trained.

Using the trained network posterior as a proposal distribution for neural importance sampling (NIS) with the exact likelihood increases sampling efficiency from $10^{-7}\text{--}10^{-3}$ (when drawing from the prior) to $5\text{--}90\%$ for cxSM parameters and $80\text{--}95\%$ for thermodynamic parameters.

Because only $\sim 0.6\%$ of the cxSM parameter space produces a detectable signal ($\text{SNR} > 1$) and strong signals lie near the boundary where the transition fails to complete, high-SNR posteriors form thin, curved degenerate strips whose thickness NPE estimates conservatively until refined by NIS.

The bubble wall velocity $v_w$ is weakly constrained in model-independent thermodynamic fits due to parameter degeneracies, but becomes much better constrained when inferred directly within a specific particle model like the cxSM where $T_n$, $\alpha$, and $\beta/H_*$ cannot vary independently.

Jointly inferring LISA instrumental noise parameters ($P$ and $A$) pins them down to $0.01\%$ and $0.2\%$ precision without degrading physical constraints, whereas networks trained at fixed noise fail when the true noise level shifts by just $1\text{--}2\%$.

ai.summary: If the early Universe underwent a first-order phase transition—where symmetry breaking happens violently through the nucleation and collision of bubbles rather than a smooth crossover—it would generate a stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) detectable by the future space-based interferometer LISA. Measuring this signal could reveal physics beyond the Standard Model, but inferring the underlying particle physics parameters with traditional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is notoriously slow because computing the bubble nucleation physics at every step is expensive, the observable spectrum is smooth and degenerate, and viable transitions occupy only a tiny sliver ($\sim 0.6\%$) of parameter space. To overcome this, the authors apply simulation-based inference (SBI)—specifically neural posterior estimation (NPE) combining a 1D convolutional embedding network with a normalizing flow—to simulated LISA spectra. They test their framework on both phenomenological thermodynamic parameters (transition temperature $T_n$, strength $\alpha$, inverse duration $\beta/H_*$, and bubble wall velocity $v_w$) and the fundamental parameters of a complex singlet scalar extension of the Standard Model (cxSM). This provides an amortized pipeline that reconstructs parameter posteriors in about a second per dataset and can be paired with importance sampling to achieve exact-likelihood accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost.

papers.title: Revealing galaxy assembly bias with luminosity-weighted marked correlations
papers.authors: Joaquin Armijo, Roberta Vasallo, L. Raul Abramo, Antonio D. Montero-Dorta
papers.abstract: We investigate whether luminosity-weighted marked correlation functions can reveal secondary halo information beyond that encoded by halo mass alone, as expected in scenarios of galaxy assembly bias. We propose a controlled null test in which galaxy luminosities follow the same mean luminosity--halo mass relation and scatter, while their residuals are either (A) uncorrelated with secondary halo properties or (B) correlated with a standardized secondary halo property, $s$. Both models have identical halo occupation, galaxy positions, luminosity function, and unweighted projected two-point correlation function, $w_p(r_p)$, so their distinction is encoded entirely in the luminosity marks. At leading order, the projected marked correlation function difference, $\Delta\mathcal{M}_p(r_p)$, scales as $\rho^2\sigma_{\log L}^2\xi_{ss}(r_p)$, where $\rho$ controls the coupling between the luminosity and secondary-property residuals, $\sigma_{\log L}$ is the scatter in log luminosity at fixed halo mass, and $\xi_{ss}$ describes the spatial correlation of the secondary property. We test this framework using a DESI-BGS mock catalogue over $0.1<z<0.4$. For the injected dependence, we detect a marked-clustering deviation over $0.11<r_p/(h^{-1}\,{\rm Mpc})<1.04$, obtaining $\chi^2=30.14$ relative to the null covariance. A one-parameter test rejects the mass-only hypothesis at greater than $5\sigma$ significance ($p=2.13\times10^{-7}$) for $|\rho|>0.63$. At fixed $\sigma_{\log L}=0.23$, correlations as weak as $|\rho|\simeq0.52$ remain detectable, with the results stable under variations in the HOD prescription and modelled galaxy selection effects. These results establish luminosity-weighted marked clustering as a sensitive null test for property-based galaxy assembly bias and secondary halo information hidden from unweighted two-point clustering.

conclusions: When galaxy luminosity residuals at fixed halo mass are coupled to a standardized secondary halo property $s$ with correlation coefficient $\rho$, the excess projected marked correlation function scales at leading order as $\Delta\mathcal{M}_p(r_p) \simeq \rho^2 \sigma_{\log L}^2 \xi_{ss}(r_p)$, where $\sigma_{\log L}$ is the log-luminosity scatter at fixed mass and $\xi_{ss}(r_p)$ is the spatial correlation of the secondary halo property.

Using DESI-BGS-like mock catalogues ($0.1 < z < 0.4$) with a log-luminosity scatter of $\sigma_{\log L} = 0.23$, the authors detect the assembly-bias signal on small scales ($0.11 < r_p / (h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}) < 1.04$), driven primarily by intra-halo (1-halo) galaxy pairs.

A one-parameter test rejects the mass-only null hypothesis at $>5\sigma$ significance ($\chi^2 = 30.14$, $p = 2.13\times 10^{-7}$) when the coupling strength is $|\rho| > 0.63$, while weaker correlations remain detectable at 95% confidence down to $|\rho| \simeq 0.52$.

The test is stable against variations in HOD stochasticity and simulated survey selection effects (such as fibre assignment), providing a clean observational diagnostic to isolate property-based assembly bias from standard halo-mass effects.

ai.summary: In standard halo occupation distribution (HOD) models, a dark matter halo's mass is assumed to be the sole property governing the number and luminosity of the galaxies it hosts, whereas "galaxy assembly bias" occurs when secondary halo properties—such as halo concentration or formation time—also influence galaxy properties at fixed mass. Detecting property-based assembly bias is notoriously tricky because models with and without it can produce the exact same galaxy positions and standard unweighted two-point correlation functions. To break this degeneracy, the authors design a controlled null test using luminosity-weighted marked correlation functions—statistics that weight galaxy pairs by the product of their luminosities—comparing a baseline mass-only model against one where luminosity scatter at fixed halo mass is correlated with halo concentration residuals. Applying this framework to mock catalogues mimicking the DESI Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS) built from the Millennium XXL $N$-body simulation, they show that marked clustering on small scales can cleanly reveal secondary halo dependencies that are completely invisible to traditional two-point clustering.

papers.title: Multiphase Gas in High-$z$ Cosmic Sheets
papers.authors: Charles Willard, Yakov Faerman, Samuel McCarty, Matthew McQuinn, Nir Mandelker, Thomas Quinn
papers.abstract: We present high-resolution cosmological simulations of individual cosmic sheets ($z=3-6$) using the moving-mesh code AREPO to study cold gas ($T\approx10^4\rm ~K$) in the diffuse cosmic web. We find cosmic sheet gas forms a fragmented morphology, evident as kiloparsec-scale variations in the neutral hydrogen column density ($N_{\rm HI}$). Fragmentation arises from the bending and disruption of the cold-dense sheet core into a multiphase medium. Nonlinear thin shell instability (NTSI) and later shear-induced vorticity drive this bending, rather than previously suggested thermal or Richtmyer-Meshkov instabilities. Higher resolution enhances fragmentation. Across a fourfold range in spatial resolution, $N_{\rm HI}$ covering fractions increase by factors of $\approx 1.5-3.5$ for partial Lyman-limit systems (pLLS) and Lyman-limit systems (LLS). An order-of-magnitude estimate suggests sheets may host a large fraction of the ultra-low metallicity (p)LLS population. Equivalent MP-Gadget simulations show qualitatively similar fragmentation, but numerical smoothing effects are present. Cosmic-sheet gas properties remain unconverged despite our high resolutions.

conclusions: Cold gas in cosmic sheets fragments via the nonlinear thin shell instability (NTSI)—which amplifies bending modes seeded by small-scale perturbations ($k > 2\pi / 100\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{ckpc}$)—followed by shear-generated vorticity and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities, rather than thermal instability.

Sheet gas properties remain numerically unconverged down to cell sizes of $\Delta x_{\rm cell} \approx 0.4\,\mathrm{pkpc}$ ($m_{\rm gas} \approx 9\times 10^3\,M_\odot$): increasing spatial resolution fourfold boosts the covering fraction of partial Lyman-limit systems (pLLSs) by $1.5\times$ in cooler sheets ($T_{\rm vir} \approx 2\times 10^5\,\mathrm{K}$) and Lyman-limit systems (LLSs) by $3.5\times$ in hotter sheets ($T_{\rm vir} \approx 8\times 10^5\,\mathrm{K}$).

Order-of-magnitude estimates at $z=4$ suggest cosmic sheets account for $\mathcal{O}(10\%)$ of all pLLSs and $\mathcal{O}(1\%)$ of LLSs, potentially making up a large fraction of the observed ultra-low-metallicity ($[\mathrm{X/H}] < -3.5$) absorber population.

Comparison with equivalent SPH (MP-Gadget) runs shows qualitatively similar fragmentation, but artificial shock broadening and phase-boundary smoothing in SPH lead to over-cooling and obscure the underlying physical instabilities compared to AREPO's Voronoi mesh.

This diffuse gas is observed in quasar spectra as neutral hydrogen ($\mathrm{HI}$) absorption features, including dense "Lyman-limit systems" (LLSs, $N_{\rm HI} > 10^{17.2}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$) and "partial LLSs" (pLLSs) that are thick enough to block hydrogen-ionizing UV radiation. The authors run a suite of idealized, small-box ($4$ and $8\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{cMpc}$) high-resolution cosmological hydrodynamic simulations using the moving-mesh code AREPO (and compare against the SPH code MP-Gadget) at $z=3\text{--}6$, seeding 1D Gaussian sheet collapse via the Zel'dovich approximation while varying the background matter power spectrum to isolate what drives kiloparsec-scale gas clumping. They demonstrate that the cold sheet core fragments due to the nonlinear thin shell instability (NTSI)—a hydrodynamic buckling of a thin shock-bounded layer—followed by shear-induced Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities, significantly boosting dense $\mathrm{HI}$ absorber counts and showing that standard cosmological simulations fail to resolve this pristine, metal-poor gas phase.

papers.title: First $Ω_{\rm m}-w$ Measurement Using Only Fast Radio Burst Observations
papers.authors: Yi-Ying Wang, Shi-Jie Gao, Chi Zhang, Yi-Zhong Fan
papers.abstract: Though fast radio bursts (FRBs) are widely advocated as a dark energy probe, no valid $\Omega_m-w$ constraint has been obtained exclusively from FRB data to date. Benefiting from a rapidly growing localized sample and a novel statistical framework for modeling the dispersion measure (DM), we report the first simultaneous inference of the matter density $\Omega_m$ and dark energy equation of state parameter $w$ from FRBs alone, without external observational priors on these two parameters. We combine a multi-parameter emulator for the nonlinear matter power spectrum with a physically motivated electron prescription to construct a cosmology-dependent cosmic-DM distribution. Within this unified analysis framework, the mean and variance of DM respond self-consistently to the same underlying cosmology, directly connecting the FRB likelihood to both cosmic expansion and structure growth. Analyzing 125 localized FRBs at $0.105\leq z\leq2.148$, we obtain $\Omega_m = 0.33^{+0.10}_{-0.11}$ and $w = -0.80^{+0.28}_{-0.38}$ under the flat $w$CDM model. We find a new positive $\Omega_m-w$ degeneracy in the FRB posterior, opposite to the strong anticorrelation derived from Type Ia supernovae, offering a complementary test of dark energy properties and highlighting their potential in future precision cosmological studies.

conclusions: Using 125 localized FRBs alone ($0.105 \le z \le 2.148$) with a BBN prior on $\omega_b$, the authors obtain the first standalone FRB constraints in flat $w$CDM: $\Omega_m = 0.33^{+0.10}_{-0.11}$ and $w = -0.80^{+0.28}_{-0.38}$, consistent with standard $\Lambda$CDM.

Because increasing $\Omega_m$ decreases the mean cosmic DM while increasing its clustering variance—whereas increasing $w$ lowers both—FRBs exhibit a positive $\Omega_m\text{--}w$ correlation ($r = +0.54$), which runs nearly orthogonal/opposite to the strong negative degeneracy of Type Ia supernovae ($r = -0.94$).

In a flat $w_0 w_a$CDM extension, FRBs alone yield broad constraints ($\Omega_m = 0.33 \pm 0.10$, $w_0 = -0.65^{+0.43}_{-0.57}$, $w_a = -0.78^{+1.26}_{-1.25}$), while combining FRBs with Planck CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+ SNe Ia yields $w_0 = -0.846^{+0.054}_{-0.053}$ and $w_a = -0.548^{+0.192}_{-0.204}$, corresponding to a $\sim 2.6\sigma$ preference for dynamical dark energy.

A key systematic limitation is that the small-scale electron bias $b_e(k,z)$ and ionized fraction are calibrated to fixed IllustrisTNG/CAMELS hydrodynamical prescriptions, meaning future analyses will need joint cosmology-and-baryonic-feedback emulators to marginalize over gas redistribution by AGN and stellar feedback.

Previous FRB dark energy studies could not constrain the matter density $\Omega_m$ and dark energy equation of state $w$ from FRBs alone because they relied on cosmic-DM probability distributions calibrated at a single fiducial cosmology, ignoring how cosmic-DM variance changes with non-linear structure growth. In this paper, the authors build a self-consistent likelihood for 125 localized FRBs ($0.105 \le z \le 2.148$) by coupling the 10-parameter GokuNEmu non-linear matter power spectrum emulator with an IllustrisTNG/CAMELS-calibrated electron bias model ($P_{ee}(k,z) = b_e^2(k,z) P_{\rm DMO}(k,z)$) to predict how both the mean and the line-of-sight variance of cosmic DM vary across cosmological parameter space. This matters because propagating cosmology into the DM scatter unlocks the first standalone FRB constraints in the $\Omega_m\text{--}w$ plane and reveals a new parameter degeneracy direction that is opposite to that of Type Ia supernovae.

papers.title: Design and Forecasts for a Rubin Twilight Program for Nearby Type Ia Supernovae
papers.authors: Xianzhe TZ Tang, Dillon Brout, Christopher W. Stubbs, Elana K. Urbach, J. Bryce Kalmbach, Greg Aldering, Bastien Carreres, Chris Frohmaier, Ayan Mitra, Erik R. Peterson, Corentin Ravoux, the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration
papers.abstract: Nearby Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are important for supernova cosmology, but saturation in 30 s exposures, gaps in light-curve sampling, and the footprint of Vera C. Rubin Observatory's baseline Wide-Fast-Deep (WFD) survey limit the nearby sample. To improve the low-$z$ sample, we propose a twilight follow-up program using Rubin Observatory for 1-5 s griz exposures at solar altitudes $-12^\circ \le \mathrm{Alt}_\odot \le -9^\circ$. Using simulations of one year of WFD observations, we find that twilight follow-up adds 230 quality-selected SNe Ia from an external sample drawn primarily from the Transient Name Server (TNS). At $z<0.08$, the usable sample increases from 368 to 643 SNe Ia, including 50 WFD events recovered by refitting their light curves with twilight photometry. Combining these twilight observations with high-redshift WFD and Deep Drilling Field samples increases the statistical-only dark-energy $(w_0,w_a)$ figure of merit from 49.3 to 58.3 (18%) and reduces $\sigma(w_a)$ by 10%. For measurements of structure growth at $0.02 \le z<0.06$, the fractional uncertainty on $f\sigma_8$ decreases from 0.783 to 0.305. Restricting the program to $-12^\circ \le \mathrm{Alt}_\odot \le -11^\circ$ reduces the dark-energy improvement to 7.2%. These short exposures could also provide unsaturated photometry of potential distance-ladder calibrators at $z<0.02$.

conclusions: Adding a twilight follow-up program ($-12^\circ \le \mathrm{Alt}_\odot \le -9^\circ$) for one year increases the usable low-redshift ($z<0.08$) SNe Ia sample from 368 to 643 events, including 230 external discoveries and 50 baseline Rubin SNe Ia rescued from poor sampling or saturation.

When combined with high-redshift Rubin samples, the augmented low-$z$ anchor increases the statistical dark energy $(w_0, w_a)$ Figure of Merit from 49.3 to 58.3 (an 18% improvement) and shrinks the uncertainty $\sigma(w_a)$ by 10% (dropping to a 7.2% FoM gain if twilight time is restricted to $-12^\circ \le \mathrm{Alt}_\odot \le -11^\circ$).

By denser sampling of peculiar velocities in the local universe ($0.02 \le z < 0.06$), the fractional uncertainty on the cosmic growth rate $f\sigma_8$ drops by more than half, from $0.783$ down to $0.305$.

Short twilight exposures prevent saturation for very nearby SNe Ia ($z<0.02$), providing same-instrument photometry of potential Cepheid/TRGB distance-ladder calibrators that is crucial for controlling cross-survey photometric calibration systematics in $H_0$ measurements.

ai.summary: Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are standardisable candles used to map the cosmic expansion history, and nearby ($z < 0.1$) supernovae are essential both for anchoring the low-redshift end of the Hubble diagram to constrain dark energy and for measuring the local growth rate of cosmic structure ($f\sigma_8$) via peculiar velocities. However, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's main Wide-Fast-Deep (WFD) survey uses 30-second exposures that saturate on bright, nearby SNe Ia and leaves sampling gaps that ruin light-curve fits. To solve this without taking away prime dark-sky survey time, the authors design and simulate a twilight follow-up program that uses Rubin for short (1–5 second) $griz$ exposures during astronomical/nautical twilight ($-12^\circ \le \mathrm{Alt}_\odot \le -9^\circ$) to target externally discovered nearby transients. This provides a large, homogeneously calibrated low-$z$ supernova sample on the exact same photometric system as Rubin's high-$z$ sample, eliminating cross-telescope calibration systematics and sharpening constraints on dynamical dark energy ($w_0, w_a$) and local structure growth.

papers.title: The Universality of Halo Growth and Merger Rates in Modified Gravity Theories
papers.authors: Haicong Xu, Yechun Yong, Feihong He, Zhongxu Zhai, Jiaxin Han, Baojiu Li
papers.abstract: In the standard $\Lambda$CDM framework, the merger rate of dark matter haloes has been found to follow a nearly universal form, with only weak dependence on halo mass and redshift. We examine whether this universality is preserved in modified gravity (MG) models, where the growth of cosmic structure can deviate from that of general relativity (GR). We use the ELEPHANT suite of large $N$-body simulations to study halo merger rates and mass accretion histories in different modified gravity models, including two representative scenarios beyond-GR: the Hu--Sawicki chameleon $f(R)$ model and the normal branch of the Dvali--Gabadadze--Porrati model. For the mass accretion histories, the modified gravitational effect can produce systematic departures from GR, generally corresponding to more rapid halo growth. The deviations are relatively small when the MG effect is weak, while they become more pronounced in models with strong deviation from GR and can exceed $15\%$ in the extreme case. For the halo merger rate, we find that the nearly universal behavior is well preserved across all the gravity models, with only weak dependence on redshift and halo mass, reflecting the unbiased accretion nature of halo growth. However, apparent deviation from this universality can arise if the halo mass is not defined consistently with the modified gravity model.

conclusions: **Faster halo assembly in modified gravity:** Because the fifth force enhances gravitational attraction when unscreened, halos of a fixed $z=0$ mass grow more rapidly at late times in MG than in GR—meaning their high-redshift progenitors were less massive, by up to $\sim 5\%$ in nDGP (N1), $>10\%$ in $f(R)$ F5, and $>15\%$ in F4.

**Universal specific merger rate:** Once normalized by logarithmic halo mass growth ($dN_{\mathrm{merge}} / d\xi / d\log M$), the halo merger rate as a function of progenitor mass ratio $\xi$ is nearly identical across GR, $f(R)$, and nDGP, with negligible dependence on redshift or host halo mass ($M_0 \ge 10^{13.2}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$). This supports the "unbiased accretion" picture where halos sweep up surrounding diffuse matter and smaller halos in fixed proportions regardless of the underlying force law.

**Subhalo-finder systematic in modified gravity:** Defining halo mass via the gravitationally bound particles identified by `HBT+` introduces an artificial, redshift-dependent break in merger-rate universality for F4 and F5. Because `HBT+` uses a standard Newtonian unbinding routine that ignores the fifth-force binding potential, it systematically underestimates bound subhalo masses in unscreened regimes—a crucial methodological caveat for building halo catalogs in MG simulations.

ai.summary: In standard $\Lambda$CDM, dark matter halos grow hierarchically in a remarkably self-similar way: once you scale out a halo's overall mass growth rate, the "specific merger rate" (the number of mergers per unit logarithmic mass gain as a function of progenitor mass ratio $\xi$) is nearly universal across redshift, halo mass, and background cosmology. This paper tests whether that universality survives in modified gravity (MG) theories where fifth forces and environmental screening alter structure formation. Using the ELEPHANT suite of $N$-body simulations—covering General Relativity (GR), Hu–Sawicki $f(R)$ gravity (F4, F5, F6, with chameleon screening), and normal-branch DGP gravity (N1, N5, with Vainshtein screening)—the authors construct halo merger trees with the history-based `HBT+` subhalo finder and track both mass accretion histories (MAHs) and merger rates. Measuring how halos assemble and merge in MG is essential for connecting non-linear simulation outputs to galaxy clustering observables and for ensuring halo finders do not introduce hidden GR biases into beyond-$\Lambda$CDM analyses.

papers.abstract: We present and analyse the results of Science Data Challenge 3b (SDC3b; this https URL ), an Epoch of Reionization (EoR) inference exercise organised by the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) using simulated SKA data. The nine-month challenge, running from October 2024 to May 2025, represents the first community-wide comparison of EoR inference pipelines on common simulated datasets. We consider multiple datasets designed to assess performance on both foreground-free and foreground-contaminated cylindrical power spectra and imaging products, adopting different reionization scenarios and EoR simulation models. We include results from 16 teams, which employ a range of methodologies to infer the posterior distribution of the hydrogen neutral fraction across three redshift intervals spanning z=8.41 to z=6.25. The results show significant inter-team variability of the astrophysical constraints even in the simpler case where only instrumental noise is added to the cosmological signal. This underscores the need for further investigation into the relative contributions of signal modelling, the treatment of instrumental effects, and inference methods to the robustness of the resulting conclusions. Although individual methods can produce biased parameter estimates, the combined average of their estimates remains close to the input values, suggesting that independent approaches can offset method-specific biases.

conclusions: Even in idealized, foreground-free datasets containing only 100 hours of SKA-Low instrumental noise and residual calibration errors, the 16 participating teams recovered substantially different astrophysical constraints, with median Z-scores (deviations from the ground truth in units of the reported uncertainty) of $(2.1, 2.2, 1.6)$ and $(1.3, 1.5, 2.1)$ across the three redshift bins for the two foreground-free mocks.

This systematic scatter is comparable to or exceeds the statistical observational uncertainty, demonstrating that individual inference pipelines severely underestimate their true error bars when they fail to budget for emulator training, prior boundaries, likelihood assumptions, and simulator modelling differences.

Using the same underlying simulation code (e.g., 21cmFAST, used by 11 teams) did not guarantee consistent results, showing that implementation details—such as prior ranges on the minimum halo mass $M_{\mathrm{min}}$, parameter space dimensionality, and emulator/SBI training strategies—are major drivers of inference bias alongside differences between physical simulators.

While individual pipelines frequently produced biased estimates of the hydrogen neutral fraction $x_{\mathrm{HI}}$, the ensemble average across all teams stayed close to the true input values, suggesting that future real SKA EoR analyses should combine multiple independent inference frameworks to mitigate method-specific biases.

ai.summary: During the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), ultraviolet radiation from the first galaxies gradually ionized the neutral hydrogen gas in the intergalactic medium, a transition that upcoming radio interferometers like the Square Kilometre Array (SKA-Low) aim to map using the redshifted 21-cm emission line. Translating an extracted 21-cm signal into physical constraints on reionization requires complex simulation-based inference or emulators, which had never been systematically benchmarked across the community on common mock data. In the SKA Science Data Challenge 3b (SDC3b), 16 independent teams blindly inferred the mean neutral hydrogen fraction $x_{\mathrm{HI}}$ across three redshift intervals ($z = 8.41$ to $6.25$) from simulated SKA-Low 2D cylindrical power spectra $P(k_\parallel, k_\perp)$ and tomographic image cubes generated with two distinct radiative transfer codes (pyC2Ray and 21cmFAST) under realistic telescope noise, calibration errors, and foreground residuals. This benchmark matters because it reveals whether current 21-cm inference pipelines can reliably recover the true reionization history and provide trustworthy error bars once SKA achieves a detection.

papers.title: Galaxy Bias and Soft Limits from Inflation
papers.authors: Charalampos Nikolis, Henrique Rubira
papers.abstract: Primordial non-Gaussianity (PNG) leaves an imprint on large-scale structure through a scale-dependent galaxy bias, and properly incorporating the effects of higher order PNG into the bias expansion requires a consistent renormalization framework that extends beyond the squeezed limit of the bispectrum. We develop the multi-loop renormalization of bias operators in the presence of non-vanishing primordial n-point functions of arbitrary order, including stochastic contributions. We show that galaxy bias renormalization is determined by the multi-soft limits of primordial correlators and bias kernels. papers.title: Sourcing vector perturbations in warm inflation through shear viscous effects
papers.authors: Arjun Berera, Suddhasattwa Brahma, Zizang Qiu, Rudnei O.Ramos
papers.abstract: Vector modes are generally believed not to play a significant role in standard cosmological perturbation theory because they decay rapidly. Non-equilibrium dynamics in the radiation bath present during warm inflation can lead to shear viscous effects, requiring a description beyond the perfect-fluid approximation. The resulting power spectrum, considered in the weak-viscosity regime, is proportional to the shear viscosity and it also depends on the Hubble slow-roll parameter $\epsilon$, decaying approximately as $a^{-(1-\epsilon)}$. This behaviour is significantly slower than the unsourced, non-viscous power spectrum, which decays as $a^{-4}$. The continuously sourced vector modes, nevertheless, decay on superhorizon scales, and the illustrative benchmark parameter choices adopted in our numerical examples give a negligible late-time vector-to-scalar ratio. Despite the absence of direct large-scale observable vector signatures, the main results establish a source of vector perturbations during warm inflation and provide a framework for studying possible secondary effects along with large-scale white noises in the vector channel.

In the formal asymptotic late-time (viscosity-dominated) limit, the dependence on the dimensionless viscosity coefficient $\alpha$ cancels between noise and damping, yielding $\mathcal{P}_{F'} \simeq \frac{2\kappa \mathcal{T}_0 k}{\pi^2 a}$, though reaching this regime requires an unphysically large number of e-folds for typical slow-roll parameters.

papers.title: Two powers, one scalar field: unified early and late dark energy
papers.authors: Bikash R. Dinda, Roy Maartens
papers.abstract: We investigate whether a single canonical scalar field can account for both early and late dark energy. Relative to flat $\Lambda$CDM, the data fit improves by $\Delta\chi^2_{\rm data}=-6.90$, or $\Delta\chi^2_{\rm objective}=-3.76$ when Gaussian parameter-prior penalties are included. The scalar-field model gives $H_0=69.53\pm0.26\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, compared with $68.45\pm0.24\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ in flat $\Lambda$CDM. This shift brings the inferred expansion rate closer to the SH0ES measurement, but does not resolve the discrepancy significantly.

papers.title: Can next generation CMB experiments discriminate between $Λ$CDM and dynamical dark energy? A Bayesian forecast for Simons Observatory and CMB-S4

papers.title: Breaking the background and linear degeneracies: Using nonlinear clustering to discriminate between dark energy models
papers.authors: Yunhao Gao, Baojiu Li, Jie Wang, Carlton M. Baugh

However, the odd-parity multipoles of the single-tracer bispectrum and the multi-tracer power spectrum, which are sensitive to leading-order relativistic corrections, break most of this degeneracy. Non-local shapes are less affected; for these, a bright-faint split of the MegaMapper-like survey improves the joint constraints on the equilateral and orthogonal shapes by a factor of $\sim2$. Finally, local relativistic effects should be detectable at SNR $\sim13$, with a bright-faint split of a DESI-like BGS survey, provided the magnification bias is known to a few per cent, but only marginally, SNR $\lesssim2.5$, for the higher-redshift surveys, and not with the single-tracer bispectrum dipole.

Including light-cone corrections requires marginalizing over the evolution bias (count slope $n_{\mathrm{evol}}$) and magnification bias ($\mathcal{Q}$), which degrades $\sigma(f_{\mathrm{NL}}^{\mathrm{loc}})$ by $\sim 50\%$–$60\%$ in even-multipole analyses; however, adding the odd-parity bispectrum dipole (which is sensitive to $\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{H}/k)$ relativistic terms) breaks the $n_{\mathrm{evol}}$ degeneracy and reduces this precision loss to $\sim 15\%$, leaving $\mathcal{Q}$ as the primary limiting nuisance parameter.

For non-local PNG shapes (equilateral and orthogonal), relativistic degeneracies are small ($\lesssim 2\%$ uncertainty degradation), and performing a bright–faint multi-tracer split in a MegaMapper-like survey improves joint power spectrum and bispectrum constraints by a factor of $\sim 2$ to $\sigma(f_{\mathrm{NL}}^{\mathrm{eq}})\approx 2.9$ and $\sigma(f_{\mathrm{NL}}^{\mathrm{orth}})\approx 4.9$.

Local relativistic projection effects are undetectable in the single-tracer bispectrum dipole ($\mathrm{SNR} < 1$, after correcting a sign error in previous literature), but can be detected at $\mathrm{SNR} \approx 13$ using a bright–faint split of a low-redshift DESI-like BGS survey (where Doppler magnification is strong), provided $\mathcal{Q}$ is known to within a few percent (or $\sim 25\%$ for a $5\sigma$ detection).

papers.title: Modeling the gravitational wave spectrum from slowly-evolving sources in the early Universe: constant-in-time and coherent-decay models
papers.authors: Antonino S. Midiri, Alberto Roper Pol, Madeline Salomé, Chiara Caprini
papers.abstract: We study the production of gravitational wave (GW) backgrounds from slowly-evolving sources in the early Universe, following the Constant-in-Time (CiT) model, presented and validated against simulations of decaying turbulence in arXiv:2201.05630 . We extend the CiT model to account for the source decay using a coherent description for the unequal-time correlator (UETC) of the source. We present a generic framework that allows us to study different types of sources. As examples, we discuss the applicability of this framework to the production of GWs from decaying MHD turbulence, sound waves, and bubble collisions in first-order phase transitions. We show that the validity of the CiT and the coherent-decay models presented in this work relies on long decorrelation times of the source. However, as the decorrelation timescale of the UETC becomes short, a resonant term grows on top of the GW spectrum predicted by the CiT model, as found, for example, in earlier analytical studies of GW production from turbulence and sound waves. This model is compatible with previous numerical results and explains why sound waves in a radiation-dominated fluid are more efficient than subrelativistic MHD turbulence in producing GWs, which is no longer the case for relativistic turbulence. The CiT model predicts a generic spectrum that scales as $k^3$ in the IR regime, develops a linear $k$ at intermediate frequencies, and decays as $k^{1-b_\Pi}$ at frequencies above the inverse correlation length scale of the source, where $b_\Pi$ is uniquely determined by the type of source and the UV slope of its spectrum. Since the $k^3$ and $k$ scalings always appear for slowly-evolving sources and they are commonly found in studies of GW production, we motivate checking the potential applicability of the CiT to other sources of GWs.

conclusions: Slowly evolving sources follow a universal GW energy density spectral shape: a causal infrared tail $\Omega_{\rm GW}(k) \propto k^3$ at large scales, an intermediate linear regime $\propto k$ (or $k^3 \ln^2(1 + \mathcal{H}_*/k)$ in an expanding radiation background), and an ultraviolet decay $\propto k^{1-b_\Pi}$ set by the small-scale anisotropic stress slope (e.g., $\propto k^{-8/3}$ for Kolmogorov turbulence with $b_\Pi = 11/3$).

The CiT approximation holds when the sourcing duration is much shorter than the source's decorrelation time ($\delta\tau_{\rm fin} \ll \delta\tau_{\rm dcorr}$); when $u_{\rm dcorr} k_* \tau_* \Upsilon \gtrsim 1$ (for turbulence) or $c_{\rm s} k_* \tau_* \Upsilon \gtrsim 1$ (for sound waves), a resonant term grows linearly with duration on top of the CiT prediction.

This decorrelation threshold resolves a discrepancy between analytical models and simulations: sound waves in a radiation fluid ($c_{\rm s}^2 = 1/3$) trigger resonant linear growth and produce GWs much more efficiently than subrelativistic MHD turbulence ($u_{\rm dcorr} \ll 1$), though relativistic turbulence restores comparable efficiency.

The new coherent-decay model smoothly suppresses the large-scale ($k \lesssim \delta\tau_{\rm dc}^{-1}$) and intermediate GW amplitude compared to the CiT model's abrupt cutoff, showing that neglecting source decay during the active phase leads to an overestimation of the low-frequency GW background.

Predicting the shape of this GW energy spectrum requires knowing the source's unequal-time correlator (UETC), a statistical measure of how the fluid or field anisotropic stresses correlate across different moments in time, which is normally only accessible via expensive 3D simulations. In this paper, the authors build a unified analytical framework (implemented in the open-source `CosmoGW` code) that models the UETC for generic velocity, magnetic, and scalar fields using two approximations: the "Constant-in-Time" (CiT) model, where the source evolves slower than the GW light-crossing time $1/k$, and a new "coherent-decay" model that accounts for the power-law decay of the source's amplitude and characteristic scale over time. This provides fast, accurate GW templates across cosmological sources and resolves a long-standing puzzle about why sound waves produce GWs much more efficiently than subrelativistic turbulence in numerical simulations.

papers.title: Star-forming disc galaxies align tangentially with the cosmic tidal field
papers.authors: Calum Murray, Roman Paviot, Martin Kilbinger, Cail Daley, Ken Ganga, Michael J. Hudson
papers.abstract: The alignments of galaxy shapes, with one another and with the large-scale structure of the Universe, have been a topic of considerable investigation within cosmology and extragalactic astrophysics for the last 60 years. Galaxy alignments are a major systematic for weak gravitational lensing and help us learn about the processes of galaxy formation. Red early-type galaxies are known to show strong radial alignments around other galaxies; however, blue star-forming galaxies have shown little evidence of alignment. We combine SPHEREx spectrophotometry with DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys to build a full-sky catalogue of 71 million galaxies with precise redshifts. With this catalogue we are able to measure alignment signals by splitting galaxies into colour and morphological samples. We detect tangential alignment of blue disc galaxies at $22.5\sigma$ and radial alignment of red spheroidal galaxies at $65\sigma$. By measuring the alignment signal separately around overdensities and underdensities, we show that each of these alignments has the scale and environmental dependence of a linear response to the cosmic tidal field; a response purely quadratic in the Gaussian tidal field, as in classic tidal torque theory is ruled out.

conclusions: **High-significance detection in blue discs:** Blue disc galaxies exhibit strong tangential alignment around galaxy overdensities ($22.5\sigma$ combined detection across $0.20 < z < 0.55$, with linear alignment amplitudes $A_1 = -2.81 \pm 0.23$ and $-3.79 \pm 0.33$), while red spheroidal galaxies show strong radial alignment ($65\sigma$ combined detection).

**Linear vs. quadratic tidal response:** By measuring alignments separately around the top 20% overdense regions (clusters) and bottom 20% underdense regions (voids), the authors find that the alignment signal flips sign—blue discs align tangentially around clusters and radially around voids (and vice versa for red spheroids). This proves the alignment is a linear response to the tidal field ($A_1 = -2.43 \pm 0.22$, $\text{PTE} = 0.80$) and rules out a purely quadratic tidal-torquing response ($\text{PTE} = 7 \times 10^{-23}$), which cannot change sign with density.

**Mass, morphology, and resolution dependence:** The alignment amplitude increases strongly with stellar mass for both blue discs and red spheroids. Selecting blue galaxies by colour alone without morphological or angular-size cuts dilutes the signal ($A_1$ drops from $-2.81$ to $-0.62$ for lower-resolution cuts), and cross-checks with DES Y6 shapes reveal that unresolved/small blue galaxies actually align radially ($A_1 > 0$), explaining why previous surveys reported null detections.

**Challenge for weak lensing and galaxy formation:** Because upcoming Stage-IV weak lensing surveys (Euclid, LSST, Roman) rely heavily on blue star-forming galaxies as lensing sources—and current hydrodynamical simulations fail to reproduce this large-scale projected tangential alignment—intrinsic alignment models in weak lensing pipelines will need careful morphological and scale-dependent calibration.

While massive red elliptical galaxies are well known to stretch radially toward matter overdensities, blue star-forming disc galaxies—which make up the majority of lensing source galaxies in surveys like Euclid—were long assumed to have negligible alignments governed at most by a weak, quadratic "tidal torquing" spin-up mechanism. In this paper, the authors combine DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys shapes and morphologies with SPHEREx spectrophotometry to build an unbiased, full-sky catalogue of 63 million galaxies ($z < 0.55$) with high-precision redshifts ($\sigma_{\mathrm{NMAD}} \approx 0.006$), measuring position–shape cross-correlations ($w_{g+}$) across colour, morphology (Sérsic index), stellar mass, and cosmic environment. They discover a striking tangential alignment of blue disc galaxies around overdensities that flips to radial alignment around cosmic voids, demonstrating that disc galaxies respond linearly to the large-scale tidal field rather than following classic quadratic tidal torque theory.

papers.title: Little Red Dots from Primordial Vacuum Bubbles
papers.authors: Miguel Barroso Varela, Katherine Freese, Matthew Kleban, Cameron Norton, Evangelos I. Sfakianakis
papers.abstract: Quantum tunneling transverse to the inflaton trajectory can produce $10^6$--$10^8M_\odot$ primordial black holes at the abundance of JWST's little red dots, without the enhanced curvature perturbations excluded by limits on CMB spectral distortions. Rare vacuum bubbles nucleate during a brief interval of inflation and later form black holes, with adjustable mass and abundance and a narrow mass spectrum of percent-level width. The leading constraint, from accretion, is satisfied for a population matching the bright little red dots even if all the emitted radiation escapes as hard X-rays.

conclusions: Tunneling in a field direction orthogonal to the slow-roll inflaton trajectory localizes bubble nucleation around a specific epoch ($N_\star \simeq 40\text{--}42$ $e$-folds before the end of inflation), producing a nearly monochromatic PBH mass spectrum with a logarithmic width of $\sigma_{\ln M} \simeq 0.04$ ($\sim 4\%$).

Unlike standard Gaussian-fluctuation PBH models, this mechanism requires no enhancement of the primordial curvature power spectrum and generates sky-averaged CMB spectral distortions of $\overline{\mu} \lesssim 6.4 \times 10^{-11}$, roughly six orders of magnitude below the COBE/FIRAS upper limit ($|\overline{\mu}| < 4.7 \times 10^{-5}$).

Post-recombination gas accretion onto these PBHs is constrained by Planck CMB anisotropy limits on exotic energy injection: a population matching the bright LRD abundance ($n_{\rm LRD} = 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$ at $M_i = 10^7 M_\odot$) is allowed even if $100\%$ of the accretion luminosity escapes as hard X-rays ($f_X = 1$), whereas matching the full LRD population ($n_{\rm LRD} = 2\times 10^{-5}\text{--}10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$) requires $f_X \lesssim 0.1\text{--}0.5$ under Eddington-limited accretion.

Because bubble nucleation events are rare and independent, the resulting PBHs are Poisson-distributed in space with a large-scale linear clustering bias of $b_{\rm PBH} \simeq 1$ and an isocurvature power spectrum at least four orders of magnitude below current CMB+BAO sensitivity.

While primordial black holes (PBHs) formed in the early universe could act as ready-made massive seeds, the standard mechanism for forming them—boosting primordial density fluctuations during inflation—is ruled out at these mass scales because the uncollapsed fluctuations dissipate as sound waves in the early photon-baryon plasma, creating prohibited spectral distortions ($\mu$-distortions) in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). To bypass this roadblock, the authors calculate a two-field inflationary model in which rare quantum tunneling events occur in a heavy scalar field perpendicular to the inflaton's slow-roll trajectory, nucleating vacuum bubbles at a specific point during inflation that later collapse into black holes upon horizon re-entry. They derive the semiclassical tunneling rate on the rolling background and test the resulting PBH population against observational bounds from CMB spectral distortions, Poisson isocurvature fluctuations, and post-recombination gas accretion. This provides a viable primordial origin for the supermassive black holes powering JWST's LRDs without altering the standard slow-roll curvature power spectrum.

papers.title: Lunar laser ranging analyses of NGLR-1 data with PEP and prospects for MPAc: towards one millimeter range precision
papers.authors: G. Bargiacchi, J. Chandler, N. Burzillà, R. Campagnola, L.Porcelli, D. Currie, J.D. Carpenter, N. Boersma, L. Cacciapuoti, P. Firme, P. Ruzza, I. Lebouteiller, C. Courde, J. Chabé, J. Eckl, S. Merkowitz, N. Colmenares, R. Reasenberg, I. Shapiro, S. Dell'Agnello
papers.abstract: Since 1969, Lunar Laser Ranging (LLR) has provided critical data for investigating Earth-Moon dynamics, lunar internal structure, and tests of General Relativity (GR). However, the measurement precision of historical arrays (such as those from Apollo and Lunokhod missions) is inherently limited by laser pulse broadening induced by lunar librations. To overcome this limit, next-generation single Cube Corner Retroreflectors (CCRs) of large optical diameter have been developed to eliminate pulse dispersion, enabling LLR measurements to advance from centimeter-level precision down to the millimeter scale. In this work, we present a detailed analysis of LLR observations from NGLR-1 (Next Generation Lunar Retroreflector-1), the first single 10cm-diameter CCR deployed on the lunar surface. Carried out using the Planetary Ephemeris Program (PEP), this study investigates individual range measurements, normal points (NPs), residuals, and observational dispersion collected by the ground stations at Apache Point Observatory Lunar laser ranging station (APOL), Wettzell, and Grasse. The results: demonstrate the success of NGLR-1 in significantly enhancing time of flight measurement precision compared to legacy Apollo and Lunokhod retroreflector arrays; indicate similar good prospects also for ESA's MPAc laser retroreflector (MoonLIGHT with Pointing Actuators) to be launched in early 2027; pave the way for a new era of LLR observations and enhanced tests of GR, alternative gravity theories in general and improved lunar geophysics and geodesy.

conclusions: Single-photon range measurements from the Wettzell station to NGLR-1 reach a one-way Earth-Moon distance precision of $\sim 6\text{ mm}$ ($\sigma \approx 21\text{ ps}$ in flight time) after second-degree polynomial detrending, reducing the residual scatter by roughly five orders of magnitude compared to raw un-detrended data.

A direct comparison at the Grasse station ($1064\text{ nm}$ over a 10-minute window) shows NGLR-1 achieves a one-way timing dispersion of $\sigma = 39.4\text{ ps}$, more than a factor of two improvement over the legacy Apollo 15 retroreflector array ($\sigma = 87.0\text{ ps}$) observed under comparable conditions.

Statistical cross-validation using RMS, Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), Durbin-Watson ($2.118$), and reduced $\chi^2$ ($1.00$) demonstrates that a 2nd-degree polynomial is optimal for stripping intra-session atmospheric and modeling drifts without overfitting physical signals.

With pulse broadening from the lunar reflector itself essentially eliminated by the single-CCR design, the current ranging precision is now bottlenecked by ground-station hardware rather than the space segment, validating the pipeline ahead of ESA's upcoming MoonLIGHT+MPAc mission in 2027.

Historically, LLR precision was limited to the centimeter scale because legacy Apollo and Lunokhod reflectors are large multi-mirror arrays: the Moon's slight wobbling (libration) tilts the array relative to Earth, causing different corners to reflect photons at slightly different distances and broadening the return pulse. To eliminate this pulse dispersion, a new generation of single, large ($10\text{ cm}$) Cube Corner Retroreflectors (CCRs)—starting with NGLR-1, which landed on the Moon in March 2025—has been deployed. In this paper, the authors use the Planetary Ephemeris Program (PEP) and a statistical polynomial detrending pipeline to analyze the first NGLR-1 ranging observations from the APOL, Wettzell, and Grasse ground stations, demonstrating that single CCRs successfully push range precision down to the few-millimeter regime and paving the way for tighter local tests of modified gravity.

papers.title: Direct inference of cosmological mass growth via timing of black hole - pulsar binaries
papers.authors: Kevin S. Croker, Gibson B. Bowling, Christopher Cain, Jake Summers, Duncan Farrah, Jeremy Coles, Hayley Williams, Chris Pearson, Joshua Grumski-Flores, Viktor T. Toth, Joshua Cohon, Rogier A. Windhorst, Leander Thiele, Gregory Tarlé, Gustavo Niz, James W. Rohlf, Nicolas Fernandez
papers.abstract: Cosmologically coupled black holes (CCBHs) respond to the expansion of the Universe, independently of conventional astrophysical processes. Recent CCBH solutions in General Relativity demonstrate evolution of gravitating mass $m_{\rm BH}\propto a^\kappa$, where $a$ is the cosmological scale factor. This can be tested through the orbital period timing of black hole (BH) pulsar (PSR) binaries. In contrast to previous methods used to constrain $\kappa$, pulsar timing measurement baselines span decades instead of gigayears, allowing sources of bias to be well-controlled. As a test case, we analyze the globular cluster BH+PSR candidate J0514--4002E (spin $P\sim 5.6~{\rm ms}$, orbital period $P_{\rm b}\sim 7~\rm days$) under the assumption that the companion is a CCBH. Taking the difference between the observed orbital and spin period derivatives removes all kinematic effects, leaving only the pulsar's intrinsic spin-down $\dot{P}_{\rm int}$ as unknown. Setting $\dot{P}_{\rm int} = 0$, its physical minimum, gives a robust upper bound $\kappa \leqslant 3.95$ at $95\%$ confidence. We estimate $\dot{P}_{\rm int}$ through the population of millisecond pulsars matched in spin and infer $\kappa = 0.82 \pm 1.67$ and $0.75 \pm 1.54$, using $H_0 = 67.6$ and $73.5\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, respectively. Adopting typical baseline scaling of timing precision, the value $\kappa = 3$, argued elsewhere to link energized vacuum BH interiors to accelerated cosmological expansion, can be excluded or detected for this $2.35^{+0.20}_{-0.18}\,M_\odot$ companion at $3\sigma$ and $5\sigma$ confidence by 2031 and 2036, respectively.

conclusions: Any cosmologically coupled black hole (CCBH) companion with mass growth $m_{\rm c} \propto a^\kappa$ induces an extra orbital period drift $\langle \dot{P}_{\rm b}^{\rm CC} / P_{\rm b} \rangle \approx -\kappa H (3 - 1/(1+q))$ via conservation of total angular momentum, while leaving other 1PN post-Keplerian parameters (periastron precession, Einstein delay, Shapiro delay) practically unaffected.

Assuming the physical minimum of zero intrinsic pulsar spin-down ($\dot{P}_{\rm int} = 0$) yields a prior-independent, conservative upper bound of $\kappa \leqslant 3.95$ ($95\%$ CL) for the $2.35\,M_\odot$ companion of PSR J0514–4002E.

Using the spin-matched Galactic field millisecond pulsar prior ($\dot{P}_{\rm int}/P = 2.0^{+0.9}_{-0.8} \times 10^{-18}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$) gives $\kappa = 0.82 \pm 1.67$ (Planck PR4 $H_0 = 67.6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$) and $\kappa = 0.75 \pm 1.54$ (local $H_0 = 73.5\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$), currently consistent with both standard decoupled black holes ($\kappa = 0$) and vacuum-energy-like coupling ($\kappa = 3$).

Because orbital period derivative uncertainties scale roughly as $T^{-2.3}$ with observing baseline $T$, continued timing of J0514–4002E alone will detect or rule out the dark-energy-motivated $\kappa = 3$ scenario at $3\sigma$ by 2031 and $5\sigma$ by 2036 (with $95\%$ probability).

papers.title: Dirac leptogenesis with charged leptons
papers.authors: Juan P. Garcés, Florian Goertz, Maya Hager
papers.abstract: Popular frameworks that explain the baryon asymmetry of the Universe (BAU) are electroweak baryogenesis, requiring a first-order phase transition, and Majorana leptogenesis, which relies on lepton number violation in the neutrino sector. Dirac leptogenesis offers an alternative mechanism that avoids both requirements, instead allowing the BAU to follow from previously generated chiral asymmetries that remain out of equilibrium in the early Universe. Conventional realizations of this scenario typically invoke ultra-light Dirac neutrinos. In this work, we generalize the mechanism to include Standard Model charged leptons by assuming that their mass-generating interactions have a UV origin and arise from higher-dimensional operators. For concreteness, the analysis is performed within a Froggatt-Nielsen setup, which allows us to naturally address fermionic mass hierarchies, too, now linked to the BAU, and we show that the proposed mechanism is viable by supercooling the flavon phase transition. The framework predicts a flavon with a (1.7-50) GeV mass, bounded by the non-observation of lepton flavor violation and the requirement for the Universe to not reheat above sphaleron temperatures, which could be indirectly probed by future lepton flavor violation experiments.

conclusions: Standard Model charged leptons ($e, \mu, \tau$) can serve as the chiral asymmetry reservoir for Dirac leptogenesis if the Froggatt–Nielsen flavor symmetry remains unbroken until after electroweak sphalerons freeze out ($T_{\mathrm{sph}} \approx 130\,\mathrm{GeV}$).

Before the flavor phase transition, left-right equilibration scales via higher-dimensional operators as $\langle \Gamma_{\mathrm{LR}} \rangle \propto T (T/\Lambda_{\mathrm{FN}})^{2n_f}$, decoupling as the Universe cools and requiring cutoff scales $\Lambda_{\mathrm{FN}} > 10^3, 10^4, 10^5\,\mathrm{GeV}$ for the electron, muon, and tau, respectively (before stronger flavor bounds are applied).

Satisfying experimental bounds on lepton flavor violation (primarily $\mu \to e\gamma$) while preventing the post-transition reheating from re-activating sphalerons requires a supercooled phase transition ($v_\Phi \gg T_{\mathrm{FN}}$) and restricts the flavon mass to $1.7\text{--}50\,\mathrm{GeV}$.

One attractive mechanism is "Dirac leptogenesis," where an early asymmetry between left- and right-handed leptons is prevented from canceling out until high-temperature electroweak processes called sphalerons convert the left-handed lepton excess into baryons; normally, this requires ultra-light right-handed Dirac neutrinos whose tiny Yukawa couplings keep left-right interactions out of thermal equilibrium. In this paper, the authors show that ordinary Standard Model charged leptons (electrons, muons, and taus) can instead act as the asymmetry reservoir if their masses arise from higher-dimensional operators in a Froggatt–Nielsen (FN) flavor model—a particle physics framework that explains fermion mass hierarchies using a new symmetry and a scalar field called a "flavon." By supercooling the flavon phase transition so that the FN symmetry breaks only after sphalerons freeze out (around $T \lesssim 130\,\mathrm{GeV}$), the charged-lepton equilibration rates are thermally suppressed at early times, protecting the baryon asymmetry while linking the cosmic matter excess directly to the Standard Model flavor puzzle.

papers.title: Subsolar neutron star-black hole binaries from collapsars: Gravitational waveform models and detectability in current searches
papers.authors: Vishal Baibhav, Valerio De Luca, Loris Del Grosso, Emanuele Berti, Brian D. Metzger, Lam Hui
papers.abstract: Detecting subsolar objects in binary mergers would be an exceptional discovery in gravitational wave astronomy. So far, dedicated searches for subsolar coalescences reported no confident detections, setting upper bounds on their merger rate. Given that standard stellar evolution is not able to produce subsolar candidates, a confident detection would point either to new physics or to unconventional astrophysical pathways. These include collapsars, where the outer parts of neutrino-cooled accretion disks around newborn stellar-mass black holes are subject to fragmentation and give rise to subsolar neutron stars, which can later merge with the central black hole. We show that current subsolar searches may miss a significant fraction of these neutron star-black hole mergers, because their templates do not account for the small mass ratios, the tidal disruption of the neutron star, and the effects of the surrounding gas. This result motivates improving the waveform modeling used in current subsolar searches and building adequate template banks tailored to these systems.

conclusions: Current LVK O4 subsolar searches miss up to $30\%$ of collapsar NS–BH events for mass ratios $q > 0.1$, and over $90\%$ of events for light neutron stars around $m_{\text{NS}} \sim 0.1\,M_\odot$ due to template mismatches in mass ratio and early termination from tidal disruption.

When accounting for negative post-Newtonian ($-4\text{PN}$) dephasing from residual accretion-disk gas ($f_{\text{disk}} = 10^{-3}$), the fraction of missed events around lighter black holes ($M_{\text{BH}} \lesssim 5\,M_\odot$) jumps from a few percent to over $50\%$.

Because these signals are both quieter (ending at Roche-lobe disruption around $f_{\text{Roche}} \simeq 65\,\text{Hz}\,(m_{\text{NS}}/0.1\,M_\odot)$ rather than reaching the ISCO) and poorly matched to vacuum templates, existing upper limits on subsolar merger rates weaken by up to two orders of magnitude ($\epsilon \sim 10^{-2}$), constraining the collapsar channel near the long gamma-ray burst rate ($\mathcal{R}_0 \simeq 80\,\text{Gpc}^{-3}\,\text{yr}^{-1}$) only around chirp masses $\mathcal{M}_c \simeq 2\,M_\odot$.

Lowering the search low-frequency cutoff from GstLAL's $45\,\text{Hz}$ to $20\,\text{Hz}$ would recover roughly $80\%$ of the $m_{\text{NS}} \simeq 0.1\,M_\odot$ events currently lost before they even enter the search band, and refiltering marginal O4 subsolar triggers with collapsar-tailored templates could boost their recovered SNR by a factor of $2\text{--}3$.
