However, an alternative astrophysical channel exists in "collapsars" (the collapsing cores of massive rotating stars that power long gamma-ray bursts), where the dense, neutrino-cooled accretion disk around a newborn black hole ($3\text{--}30\,M_\odot$) can fragment into neutron-rich clumps that form subsolar neutron stars ($0.01\text{--}1\,M_\odot$). The authors construct a frequency-domain gravitational waveform model (`NSBHc`) for these subsolar neutron stars inspiraling into their central black holes, incorporating extreme mass ratios ($q \sim 10^{-3}\text{--}10^{-1}$), huge tidal deformabilities ($\Lambda \sim 10^{10}$), early signal cutoff from tidal disruption (shredding at the Roche limit before reaching the innermost stable circular orbit), and gas-driven migration dephasing. By computing how well current LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) O4 search templates match these realistic signals, they show that current PBH-focused template banks miss the vast majority of light collapsar mergers, motivating dedicated template banks and lower frequency cutoffs.

papers.title: EuclidFM: Foundation Model for Compact Photometric Survey Representation
papers.authors: Reyhaneh Vojoudi Salmani, Mahsa Berahman, Saeed Ansarifard, Michael M. Fausnaugh, Seyed Mohammad Sadegh Movahed
papers.abstract: We present EuclidFM, a compact self-supervised model that learns object-level representations from heterogeneous catalogue photometry in Euclid Quick Data Release 1. Using 90,258 sources across three Euclid Deep Fields, a masked-autoencoder Transformer reconstructs withheld fluxes and uncertainties from available measurements, producing a 128-dimensional embedding per source. The embeddings encode morphological and photometric information: sources with high point-like probability have, on average, 12.4 similarly classified neighbours among their 15 nearest neighbours, compared with 4.3 under field- and magnitude-stratified randomization. Linear models trained on frozen embeddings predict VIS magnitudes with correlations of 0.954-0.980 across three held-out fields. For sources with VIS aperture-flux uncertainties up to 1 microJy, incorporating embeddings reduces the root-mean-square error in predicted log uncertainty by at least 24% relative to a magnitude-only model. A classifier trained on spectroscopically confirmed sources identifies 1,150 quasar candidates, but only 21 of the 156 candidates with accepted external counterparts show AGN evidence, including 12 spectroscopic quasars. The classifier's transferability to the wider photometric catalogue therefore remains uncertain, and its purity and completeness require further evaluation. Independently of classification, EuclidFM provides a common representation for downstream survey analyses when photometric coverage differs between sources. Code and data are available at this https URL .

conclusions: The 128-dimensional embeddings naturally capture apparent morphology and brightness without explicit labels: sources with high point-like probability ($P_{\rm point} \ge 0.8$) share an average of 12.4 similarly point-like neighbours among their 15 nearest neighbours in embedding space (compared to 4.3 under a field- and magnitude-matched random baseline), and linear readouts predict held-out VIS $I_{\rm E}$ magnitudes with Spearman rank correlations of $0.954$–$0.980$.

Beyond overall brightness, the representations encode information about measurement quality: for sources with VIS aperture-flux uncertainties $\sigma_I \le 1\,\mu\mathrm{Jy}$, adding the frozen embeddings to a magnitude-only model reduces the root-mean-square error in predicted log flux uncertainty by $24\%$–$37\%$ across held-out fields.

A supervised multilayer perceptron trained on a bright, class-balanced reference sample (9,675 sources) achieves $97.3\%$ test accuracy and identifies 462 stellar candidates in the wider catalogue with $99.4\%$ confirmation among Gaia DR3 matches (359 of 361 sources).

However, out-of-distribution generalization to rare classes in the fainter, galaxy-dominated general catalogue is poor: of 1,150 identified quasar candidates, only 21 of the 156 candidates with external counterparts show AGN or quasar evidence, demonstrating that classifiers trained on selective reference samples struggle to transfer directly to unlabelled survey populations.
ai.relevance_reason: While this paper uses Euclid Q1 catalogue data, it focuses on self-supervised representation learning for heterogeneous tabular photometry and star/quasar classification rather than cosmological theory, N-body simulations, beyond-$\Lambda$CDM emulators, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: Wide-field galaxy surveys like Euclid combine space-based and ground-based photometry from multiple telescopes (such as DECam, HSC, and Pan-STARRS), resulting in heterogeneous catalogues where different objects have different available wavelength bands, depths, and measurement types. To handle missing channels without discarding incomplete sources, the authors introduce EuclidFM, a compact self-supervised masked-autoencoder Transformer trained on 90,258 sources from Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1). By randomly masking 20 available flux-uncertainty pairs per object and training the network to reconstruct them from the remaining visible measurements (out of 94 possible photometric channels), the encoder compresses each source into a unified 128-dimensional summary vector (embedding). This provides a common, fixed-length feature space for downstream survey tasks—such as object classification or photometric quality estimation—even when photometric coverage varies across the sky.

papers.title: The Cosmic Infrared Background from Population III.1 Supermassive Stars and Black Holes
papers.authors: Emir Tataroglu, Jonathan C. Tan, Rosalia D. O'Brien, Devesh Nandal
papers.abstract: We investigate the cosmic infrared background (CIB) that is expected to arise from the Population (Pop) III.1 supermassive black hole (SMBH) formation scenario, which involves early SMBH seeding via supermassive primordial star formation enabled by dark matter annihilation heating. We model the emission from Pop III.1 supermassive stars, including their growth phase, flash ionization phase, and early black hole accretion phase, as well as accompanying emission from lower-mass Pop III.2 stars. The CIB is composed of stellar and SMBH accretion disk continuum radiation, nebular continuum emission, and Ly$\alpha$ radiation redistributed through scattering in the neutral intergalactic medium. Based on the feedback regulated Pop III.1 model of Petkova et al. (2026), our fiducial model assumes $\sim 10^5\,M_\odot$ Pop III.1 stars forming by $z_{\rm flash}=20$ with a comoving number density of $\sim0.2\,{\rm cMpc}^{-3}$. For this model, the combined stellar contribution is less than $1\%$ of existing direct and diffuse CIB measurements. However, the contribution to the CIB from $z\sim6-20$ SMBH accretion is expected to be larger than the Pop III.1 stellar component for average Eddington ratios $\lambda_{\text{Edd}} \sim 0.01$. Latest CIB observations place constraints of $\lambda_{\text{Edd}} \lesssim 0.3$ for the fiducial Pop III.1 model during these epochs.

conclusions: For the fiducial Pop III.1 model ($10^5\,M_\odot$ stars at $z_{\rm flash}=20$ with comoving density $n_{\rm III.1} = 0.2\,{\rm cMpc}^{-3}$ and a $10\,{\rm Myr}$ ionizing lifetime), the combined Pop III.1 and III.2 stellar emission is $<1\%$ ($2\text{--}4$ orders of magnitude below) existing direct and diffuse near/mid-infrared CIB measurements, meaning primordial stars alone cannot explain the observed CIB excess.

The stellar EBL spectrum exhibits two distinct diagnostic features if the flash ionization occurs at $z_{\rm flash}=20$: a sharp blue cutoff at $\lambda \simeq 1.85\text{--}1.92\,\mu{\rm m}$ (the redshifted Lyman limit) and a narrow spike at $\lambda \simeq 2.6\text{--}2.7\,\mu{\rm m}$ from scattered $\text{Ly}\alpha$ photons, alongside a flat mid-infrared tail ($\lambda \gtrsim 6\,\mu{\rm m}$) from the cooler ($6000\,{\rm K}$) $30\,{\rm Myr}$ protostellar growth phase.

Early AGN accretion onto the resulting SMBH seeds between $z=20$ and $z=6$ grows exponentially with the Eddington ratio $\lambda_{\rm Edd}$ and dominates over the stellar contribution for $\lambda_{\rm Edd} \gtrsim 0.01$, varying the EBL intensity by $\sim 4$ orders of magnitude between $\lambda_{\rm Edd}=0.01$ and $0.5$.

Comparing with recent optical/near-IR EBL limits (including New Horizons and COBE/DIRBE) and the $z=6$ SMBH mass budget ($\langle M_{\rm BH}\rangle \lesssim 10^7\,M_\odot$, requiring a mass growth factor $f_{\rm grow} \lesssim 100$) constrains the average Eddington ratio of these early SMBH seeds to $\lambda_{\rm Edd} \lesssim 0.3$ (or $\lesssim 0.25$ for an elevated seed density of $n_{\rm III.1} = 2.0\,{\rm cMpc}^{-3}$).
ai.summary: Direct measurements of the Cosmic Infrared Background (CIB)—the accumulated infrared glow from all cosmic sources across history—consistently exceed the total light counted from resolved galaxies, prompting debate over whether the missing diffuse flux comes from extremely distant, metal-free first-generation ("Population III") stars. This paper investigates a specific supermassive black hole (SMBH) seeding scenario in which the very first primordial stars ("Pop III.1") are heated by WIMP dark matter annihilation, allowing them to grow into $\sim 10^5\,M_\odot$ supermassive stars that trigger a brief "flash ionization" of the Universe at $z \sim 20$ before collapsing into SMBHs. The authors analytically model the near- and mid-infrared background produced during the stars' cooler protostellar growth phase, their hot ionizing flash phase, the accompanying lower-mass Pop III.2 stellar population, and subsequent accretion onto the remnant SMBHs down to $z=6$. By tracking direct continuum radiation, nebular recombination emission, and $\text{Ly}\alpha$ photons scattered by the neutral intergalactic medium, they test whether this SMBH-seeding mechanism can explain the unresolved CIB excess or is already constrained by background light measurements from COBE/DIRBE and New Horizons.

papers.title: Dark Matter Model Implications of a Candidate Sub-halo Near the Sun, and the Data Needed to Discriminate Among Them
papers.authors: Stefano Profumo, Sukanya Chakrabarti
papers.abstract: Pulsar-timing accelerations point to a localized mass concentration near the Sun, consistent with a dark matter sub-halo. We work out what such an object implies for the nature of dark matter, organizing the implications by their observable effect: suppression or enhancement of structure formation, internal structure and survival after formation, and emission or scattering by the constituents. We discuss ultralight wave dark matter, thermal and nonthermal warm dark matter, dark acoustic oscillations and dark matter-baryon scattering, elastic and inelastic self-interactions, invisible decays with recoil, primordial black holes, indirect detection, and a possible connection to the LUX-ZEPLIN high-energy recoil candidate. We then ask what new data would discriminate among these models. The existing accelerations are measured outside the tidal radius, where they are blind to the interior mass distribution, to the object's velocity, and to the sub-halo population. We identify four routes that lift these degeneracies: accelerations measured inside the halo, which separate point-mass, cuspy, and cored profiles; lensing and accretion, which test whether the mass is compact; the morphology of annihilation or decay emission, which probes the inner profile; and a search for a comoving stellar population, which tests whether the object is dark and measures its velocity. We also contrast this program with pulsar-timing-array searches for transiting dark matter substructure, which probe vastly lighter objects through a different observable.

conclusions: All pulsar endpoints and the Sun lie outside the candidate's illustrative tidal radius ($r_t \approx 0.31\,\mathrm{kpc}$, with the nearest pulsar at $0.388\,\mathrm{kpc}$); by the shell theorem, current acceleration data only measure the total enclosed mass and leave the scale radius unconstrained ($r_s = 61^{+274}_{-44}\,\mathrm{pc}$).

Correcting density unit conversions and volume factors in the original search reduces the prior-predictive probability of finding a $10^7\,M_\odot$ sub-halo in five search volumes (at a local sub-halo fraction $f_{\rm sub} = 0.03$) from $\sim 5\%$ to $\approx 0.34\%$.

If the object's mass history is matched to primordial structure suppression scales, it corresponds to fuzzy dark matter masses around $m_{\rm match}^F \sim (1.7\text{--}3.3) \times 10^{-20}\,\mathrm{eV}$ or thermal warm dark matter masses around $m_{\rm match}^W \sim 5.6\text{--}7.4\,\mathrm{keV}$, though tidal stripping prevents a single sub-halo from setting a strict mass-function cutoff.

For self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) at $\sigma/m = 1\,\mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}$, the characteristic scattering timescale is $t_s \sim 0.16\,\mathrm{Gyr}$, meaning the candidate could be in either a core-expansion or gravothermal core-collapse phase, while invisible decays with recoil kicks of tens of $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ would significantly alter its structure and survival.

Breaking the degeneracy between compact objects, cored profiles, and cuspy halos requires new interior or multi-messenger observations: pulsar accelerations measured inside $r_t$, microlensing and accretion tests, spatial morphology of indirect-detection signals ($J_{\rm ROI} \sim 1.14 \times 10^{23}\,\mathrm{GeV^2\,cm^{-5}}$), or searches for a comoving stellar population.
ai.relevance_reason: While the paper touches on small-scale transfer functions and dark matter halo structure, it focuses on Galactic pulsar-timing substructure and dark matter microphysics rather than cosmological N-body simulations, emulators, modified gravity, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: By tracking the orbital period drift of binary pulsars, astronomers can measure line-of-sight gravitational accelerations in the Milky Way and search for localized dark matter sub-halos without relying on luminous tracers. A recent analysis reported a candidate sub-halo of mass $\sim 10^7\,M_\odot$ at a distance of $0.78\,\mathrm{kpc}$ from the Sun, and this paper systematically evaluates what such an object—if confirmed—would imply for the microphysics of dark matter across models like fuzzy dark matter, warm dark matter, self-interacting dark matter (SIDM), and primordial black holes. The authors perform a rigorous geometric and statistical audit of the pulsar acceleration data, showing that because all currently measured pulsars and the Sun lie outside the object's illustrative tidal radius ($r_t \approx 0.31\,\mathrm{kpc}$), the shell theorem renders existing data completely blind to the sub-halo's internal density profile. They then map out the conditional implications of various dark sector mechanisms on the halo's formation and survival, and identify four concrete observational routes—interior pulsar accelerations, lensing/accretion, gamma-ray annihilation or decay morphology, and searches for bound stars—needed to break the profile degeneracies and distinguish among dark matter models.

papers.title: Direct simulation Monte Carlo for dark matter production and phase-space evolution
papers.authors: Felix Kahlhoefer, Ann Cathrin Wesener
papers.abstract: To study the early-universe production of dark matter particles beyond thermal equilibrium often requires solving several coupled Boltzmann equations at the phase-space level. We present a new method to address this challenge using Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) based on stochastic interactions of an ensemble of particles. We implement and validate efficient algorithms to describe freeze-out, decays, elastic scattering and number-changing processes within the dark sector. These algorithms do not require a discretisation of momentum space on a pre-defined grid and do not rely on approximations such as thermally averaged cross sections. As illustrative example, we consider a scenario with two-step dark matter production, leading to a bimodal phase-space distribution, and consider the subsequent evolution under elastic and number-changing processes. We show that DSMC is a flexible approach to explore out-of-equilibrium processes and solve Boltzmann equations at the phase-space level in order to predict the abundance of dark matter particles and their effect on structure formation.

conclusions: The authors extend the No-Time-Counter (NTC) stochastic collision algorithm within Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) to handle general $n \leftrightarrow m$ particle interactions, specifically validating freeze-out, decay, elastic $2 \leftrightarrow 2$, and number-changing $2 \leftrightarrow 3$ processes against analytical and moment-based Boltzmann solutions.

In a two-step dark matter production scenario (producing a bimodal momentum distribution from early in-equilibrium and late out-of-equilibrium decays of a parent scalar), number-changing $2 \leftrightarrow 3$ self-interactions efficiently convert the high kinetic energy of the late-decay population into rest mass, increasing the final dark matter number density while cooling the distribution.

The Monte Carlo statistical uncertainty scales as $1/\sqrt{N}$ with the number of simulation particles $N$, and an ensemble of order $N \sim 10^5$ particles is sufficient to reach observational precision without needing to pre-define a momentum-space grid.

The resulting particle sample directly represents the final non-thermal phase-space distribution and can be fed into linear Boltzmann codes (like CLASS) via Monte Carlo integration to compute small-scale matter power spectrum suppression.
ai.summary: When dark matter (DM) is produced in the early universe via very weak interactions—such as "freeze-in" or out-of-equilibrium decays rather than standard thermal freeze-out—its momentum distribution $f(p,t)$ can become highly non-thermal or even multi-peaked (bimodal), which alters how free-streaming suppresses small-scale cosmic structure. Tracking this evolution requires solving the full, unintegrated Boltzmann equation at the phase-space level, which is computationally expensive on fixed momentum grids whenever particle momenta span several orders of magnitude. To overcome this, the authors adapt Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC)—a stochastic particle-based method borrowed from rarefied gas dynamics—to simulate an ensemble of particles undergoing redshifting, decays, elastic $2 \leftrightarrow 2$ scatterings, and number-changing $2 \leftrightarrow 3$ self-interactions in an expanding homogeneous universe. They apply this grid-free approach to a two-step DM production toy model where a heavy scalar freezes out and decays into DM in two stages, demonstrating that DSMC accurately captures how subsequent self-interactions reshape and thermalise a bimodal phase-space distribution.

papers.title: Resonant Cavity Searches for Millicharged Dark Matter
papers.authors: Miguel González Albert, Ariel Arza, Saarik Kalia
papers.abstract: A plethora of resonant cavity experiments have been designed to search for ultralight dark matter (DM) candidates, such as axion or dark-photon DM. In this work, we show that these same apparatuses can be sensitive to ultralight millicharged dark matter (mDM) with masses $m_\phi\sim1-100\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$. Similar to axion DM, in the presence of a background magnetic field, mDM acts as an effective current which can excite the modes of a resonant cavity. Importantly, for a cylindrical cavity, axion DM dominantly couples to the transverse magnetic (TM) modes, whereas mDM dominantly couples to the transverse electric (TE) modes. We project the sensitivity to mDM that resonant cavity experiments can achieve if they are able to tune and readout their TE modes. We find that fractional millicharges as small as $\epsilon_m=e_m/e\sim10^{-19}$ can be probed. If mDM constitutes only a subfraction $f_\mDM \lesssim0.2\%$ of the total DM density, competing astrophysical bounds do not apply. In this case, resonant cavities can be the most sensitive probes of mDM in this mass range.

conclusions: In a cylindrical cavity with an axial magnetic field, scalar millicharged dark matter generates an azimuthal current that leaves the standard axion-search $\mathrm{TM}_{010}$ mode untouched, instead resonating predominantly with the $\mathrm{TE}_{011}$ mode at frequency $\omega = 2m_\phi$ (with spatial overlap form factor $C_{\mathrm{mDM}}^{(011)} = 0.22$).

Recasting existing axion haloscope sensitivities (such as ADMX, HAYSTAC, and CAPP) to $\mathrm{TE}_{011}$ mode searches shows they could probe fractional charges as tiny as $\epsilon_m \equiv e_m/e \sim 10^{-19}$ in narrow mass windows around $m_\phi \sim 1\text{--}100\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$.

Because early-Universe proton-scattering and astrophysical magnetic-field bounds disappear when millicharged particles make up less than $f_{\mathrm{mDM}} \lesssim 0.2\%$ of the total dark matter density, TE-tuned resonant cavities would become the most sensitive overall probes in this subcomponent regime.

Wave distortion and screening of the millicharged dark matter background by the laboratory's $\sim 7\,\mathrm{T}$ magnet or Earth's geomagnetic field remain negligible as long as $e_m \lesssim 7 \times 10^{-16}$, safely above the projected sensitivity floor of cavity searches.
ai.summary: Ultralight dark matter particles with masses well below $1\,\mathrm{eV}$ have such high phase-space number densities that they behave like coherent classical waves rather than individual particles. While resonant microwave cavity experiments ("haloscopes" like ADMX and HAYSTAC) are traditionally built to detect ultralight axions converting into photons inside a strong static magnetic field, this paper explores how those exact same detectors can search for ultralight millicharged dark matter (mDM)—hypothetical scalar particles carrying a tiny fraction $\epsilon_m = e_m/e$ of the electron's electric charge. The authors derive the modified Maxwell equations for a coherent mDM wave in a uniform axial magnetic field, showing that it acts as an oscillating azimuthal effective current at twice the particle's mass frequency ($\omega = 2m_\phi$). Crucially, because this current circulates azimuthally around the cylinder rather than flowing along the magnetic field axis like an axion-induced current, it has zero overlap with the standard transverse-magnetic ($\mathrm{TM}_{010}$) modes used in axion searches and instead excites transverse-electric ($\mathrm{TE}_{011}$) cavity modes. This means existing haloscopes could open a powerful new discovery window for millicharged dark matter simply by tuning and reading out their TE modes.

papers.title: Neutral hydrogen in the Shapley Supercluster core II. Gas content and star formation in the filaments connecting the core
papers.authors: Lwandile Gwebushe, Tiziana Venturi, Paola Merluzzi, Giovanni Busarello, Oleg Smirnov, Viviana Casasola, Francesco La Barbera, Mpati Ramatsoku, James Dawson
papers.abstract: We investigate the neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) content of galaxies across the Shapley Supercluster (SSC) at z = 0.048 by combining new deep MeerKAT L band observations of five filament pointings with archival MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey observations of the supercluster core. Together with optical data from the Shapley Supercluster Survey, these observations provide a homogeneous view of galaxy evolution from the virialised cluster environment to the surrounding filaments. We compare the HI content, star formation activity, gas depletion timescales, and morphological properties of galaxies relative to the gas fraction and star forming main sequences. The global HI detection fraction increases from 30 per cent in the cluster centre to 45 per cent in the filaments. While HI detected galaxies in the cluster centre are dominated by transition zone systems, the filament population is shared nearly equally between star forming main sequence and transition zone detections, indicating ongoing environmental transformation. Their gas properties also differ: cluster galaxies exhibit progressively depleted HI reservoirs towards the red sequence, whereas filament galaxies remain primarily gas rich. Within the filaments, long HI depletion timescales exceeding the Hubble time are concentrated in specific populations, notably 71 per cent of transition zone and 57 per cent of gas rich detections, indicating the inefficient conversion of atomic gas into stars. The HI detected filament population is dominated by late type galaxies, while the underlying non detected population is primarily composed of early type systems, consistent with environmental pre processing before cluster infall.

conclusions: The $\text{H}\,\textsc{i}$ detection fraction increases from $\sim 30\%$ in the virialised cluster centre to $\sim 45\%$ in the surrounding filaments (down to a mass limit of $M_{\textsc{Hi}} \sim 3.1\times 10^8\,\text{M}_\odot$), directly demonstrating progressive atomic gas removal as environmental density increases.

While $\text{H}\,\textsc{i}$-detected galaxies in the cluster core are dominated by quenching transition-zone systems, filament detections are split nearly evenly between the star-forming main sequence and the transition zone, showing that galaxies in filaments are already further along the quenching path than typical field galaxies.

About $71\%$ of transition-zone and $57\%$ of gas-rich filament detections have gas depletion timescales exceeding the Hubble time ($t_{\text{dep}} > 13.8\,\text{Gyr}$), meaning they retain large atomic hydrogen reservoirs that are being converted into stars very inefficiently.

These long depletion times alongside a large underlying population of $\text{H}\,\textsc{i}$-undetected early-type galaxies in the filaments point to environmental "pre-processing" via starvation (cutting off fresh cold gas accretion) operating well outside the cluster virial radius before cluster infall.
ai.summary: As galaxies fall from the cosmic web into massive galaxy clusters, environmental processes shut down their star formation ("quenching") by stripping or cutting off their supply of cold gas, particularly neutral atomic hydrogen ($\text{H}\,\textsc{i}$), the primary fuel reservoir extending well beyond a galaxy's optical disc. To test how much of this transformation happens before galaxies ever cross a cluster's virial radius ("pre-processing"), the authors combine new deep MeerKAT radio observations of five cosmic web filament pointings with archival data of the dense core of the Shapley Supercluster ($z \approx 0.048$), the most massive collapsing supercluster in the local Universe. By cross-matching 284 $\text{H}\,\textsc{i}$-detected galaxies (127 in the core, 157 in the filaments) with optical spectroscopy, they compare atomic gas reservoirs, star formation rates, morphologies, and gas depletion timescales across a continuous density gradient. This provides clear observational evidence that cosmic web filaments actively pre-process galaxies via "starvation"—suppressing their star formation efficiency while leaving much of their atomic gas intact—long before rapid gas stripping takes over inside the virialised cluster core.

papers.title: Worldsheet Effective Theory of Abelian-Higgs Cosmic Strings beyond Nambu--Goto
papers.authors: Sergio Alameda-Calvo, Josu C. Aurrekoetxea, Jose J. Blanco-Pillado, Alberto García Martín-Caro, J.M. Queiruga
papers.abstract: Cosmic strings can support long-lived excitations confined to their cores, opening channels for energy exchange with the transverse Goldstone modes that describe the string's motion. We derive a covariant worldsheet theory of their coupled dynamics directly from the Abelian-Higgs model at critical coupling, with all interaction coefficients fixed by the microscopic theory. The resulting action, which we validate against numerical lattice field theory simulations, extends the Nambu--Goto description to include a massive scalar shape mode and a massive vector mode. Dualizing the vector reveals a geometric distinction: the shape scalar mode couples to intrinsic worldsheet curvature, while the pseudoscalar couples to normal bundle curvature. These interactions explain the distinct parametric instabilities observed in lattice simulations and predict how the relative polarization of colliding transverse waves controls the excitation of the two internal modes. Our results connect microscopic string structure to the nonlinear worldsheet dynamics, providing a predictive framework for cosmic strings beyond the Nambu--Goto approximation.

conclusions: At critical coupling ($\beta = \lambda/e^2 = 1$), the bound scalar shape mode and vector gauge mode share a degenerate worldsheet rest mass $\omega_b \simeq 0.882\,e\eta$ (below the bulk radiation threshold $m_H = m_A = e\eta$), and all effective worldsheet couplings ($\kappa_S \approx 1.20$, $\kappa_V \approx 2.72$, $g_{SV} \approx 0.086$) are fixed analytically by transverse integrals of the vortex profiles with zero free parameters.

Dualizing the 2D worldsheet vector mode into a pseudoscalar $\vartheta$ reveals a clean geometric split: the scalar shape mode $\chi$ couples to the intrinsic worldsheet Ricci curvature ($\kappa_S \chi \mathcal{R}$), whereas the pseudoscalar couples to the normal bundle curvature or twist ($\omega_b \kappa_V \vartheta \mathcal{T}$).

These distinct geometric couplings explain why an excited shape mode parametrically amplifies planar transverse string waves while an excited vector mode generates helical deformations, though both instabilities share the same leading growth rate at equal normalized amplitude.

Adaptive-mesh lattice simulations of colliding transverse waves confirm the EFT predictions: how much energy transfers into scalar versus vector core excitations depends directly on the relative polarization of the colliding waves, while smooth, wide wave collisions exponentially suppress internal mode production.
ai.summary: Cosmic strings—one-dimensional topological defects that can form during symmetry-breaking phase transitions in the early universe—are usually modeled as infinitely thin relativistic wires using the Nambu–Goto action, which tracks only their transverse motion through space. However, realistic field-theory strings have a finite core thickness that can trap massive internal vibrations, providing an energy sink that causes string evolution to deviate from pure Nambu–Goto predictions. In this paper, the authors study vortex strings in the Abelian-Higgs model (a $U(1)$ gauge field coupled to a complex scalar field) at critical coupling, where the string core supports two long-lived internal bound states: a scalar "shape" mode (radial breathing of the core) and a massive vector mode (gauge polarization along the string). By expressing the 4D field theory in coordinates adapted to the string's 2D spacetime trajectory (the worldsheet) and integrating out the perpendicular directions, they derive a parameter-free 2D Effective Field Theory (EFT) and validate it against 3D adaptive-mesh lattice simulations. This provides a rigorous microscopic bridge showing exactly how a string's bending and twisting exchange energy with its internal core structure.

papers.title: Multimessenger constraints on the origin of long gamma-ray bursts with plateaus: three cases
papers.authors: Aleksander Łukasz Lenart, Maria Giovanna Dainotti, Maurice van Putten, Shigehiro Nagataki, Nissim Fraija, Agnieszka Pollo, Dieter H. Hartmann
papers.abstract: The central engines of long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) with X-ray plateaus remain uncertain. They involve a magnetar or black hole (BH), powered by spin energy and/or accretion. We examine how gravitational waves (GWs) discriminate between these scenarios. For collapsars, we consider three models: (A) a prompt phase powered by hyper-accretion onto a BH, followed by a spin-down-powered plateau; (B) a prompt phase powered by BH spin-down; and (C) a magnetar powering both the prompt and plateau phases. Each predicts a distinct GW signature in timing, energy, and frequency, ranging from broadband emission to a coherent descending chirp. We fit the selected X-ray plateaus of Swift GRBs using the model (A). For GRB~080319C, GRB~111209A, and GRB~130925A, we obtain BH masses of $M_{\rm BH}\sim24$--$124\,M_\odot$, with disc masses of $\sim10\%\,M_{\rm BH}$ at the end of the prompt phase. Mass-scaling of numerical simulations of disc emission yields GW strains of $\sim1.5-1.8\times10^{-24}$ at few hHz. This emission should be detectable by Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope, with an inferred rate from $0.5$ to $1.5$ yr$^{-1}$. However, ultra-long GRBs powered by tidal disruption events are expected to emit GWs at frequencies ranging from millihertz to decihertz, potentially within the sensitivity range of DECIGO and/or Big Bang Observer (BBO). Current or future detectors may detect GWs associated with BH-powered GRB, but magnetar engines, require next-generation detectors. Current and future detectors could map LGRB central-engine activity.

conclusions: **Three distinct GW signatures:** A prompt GRB phase driven by hyper-accretion onto a black hole followed by spin-down in a magnetically arrested disc (MAD) produces broadband, stochastic-like GWs throughout the prompt phase, whereas suspended-accretion spin-down produces a coherent descending-frequency chirp during the prompt phase, and a magnetar engine produces a lower-amplitude descending chirp that peaks early in the plateau phase.

**Inferred black hole and disc masses:** Fitting the black hole spin-down plateau model to three bright *Swift* events (GRB 080319C, GRB 111209A, and GRB 130925A) yields heavy central black hole masses of $M_{\rm BH} \approx 24\text{--}124\,M_\odot$ and minimum accretion disc masses of $M_{\rm disc} \approx 2.9\text{--}12.0\,M_\odot$ ($\sim 10\%\,M_{\rm BH}$) at the start of the plateau.

**Detectability with 3G interferometers:** Pessimistic efficiency assumptions ($\epsilon = 0.1$) give characteristic GW strains of $h_{200\,{\rm Hz}} \approx (1.5\text{--}1.8) \times 10^{-24}$, which is far below Advanced LIGO sensitivity but on the threshold of Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope (rising to $h_c \sim 2 \times 10^{-23}$ in optimistic scenarios), implying an expected detection rate of $\sim 0.5\text{--}1.5\,\text{yr}^{-1}$.

**Testing ultra-long GRB origins:** If ultra-long GRBs (durations $>10^3\,\text{s}$) are powered by white dwarf tidal disruption events around intermediate-mass black holes rather than massive-star collapsars, their GW emission shifts down to the $\text{mHz}\text{--}\text{dHz}$ band, making them targets for space-based detectors like LISA, DECIGO, and BBO.
ai.summary: Long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) are extreme relativistic explosions triggered by the core collapse of massive stars ("collapsars"), often followed by an enigmatic "X-ray plateau" where the afterglow brightness stays nearly constant for minutes to hours instead of fading away. Astronomers still debate what "central engine" powers this sustained energy injection: a rapidly spinning, highly magnetized neutron star (a magnetar) or a newborn black hole extracting rotational energy via a surrounding accretion disc. In this paper, the authors compare three physical engine models and show that each predicts a distinct gravitational wave (GW) signature in timing and frequency—ranging from a stochastic broadband burst generated by turbulent disc instabilities to a coherent "descending chirp" (a GW signal whose frequency drops over time as the central object spins down). By fitting a black hole spin-down model to the X-ray light curves of the most promising *Swift* satellite GRBs, they estimate the black hole and accretion disc masses and scale numerical simulation results to predict the resulting GW strain amplitudes. This matters because while electromagnetic observations alone struggle to break the degeneracies between central engine models, third-generation GW observatories like Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope should be sensitive enough to directly detect these accretion-disc GWs and identify what powers LGRBs.

papers.title: Inhomogeneous Cutoff Regularization of Loops in Cosmological Correlators
papers.authors: Jacopo Fumagalli, Keisuke Inomata
papers.abstract: We revisit the use of cutoff regularization in computing loop corrections to cosmological correlators. We argue that a cutoff corresponding to a fixed physical scale must be defined with respect to the local background geometry. In the presence of superhorizon perturbations, this is naturally implemented within the separate universe picture, where different local patches are regulated at the same physical scale. Expanding this cutoff in the long-wavelength background generates a series of regulator-induced contributions to loop amplitudes, which admit a diagrammatic interpretation as long-mode insertions on the corresponding loop contractions. Our cutoff prescription preserves residual spatial dilatations and volume-preserving anisotropic rescalings. It is therefore particularly relevant for loop correlators with soft external modes. We illustrate the mechanism by computing the contributions to the one-loop scalar and tensor power spectra on superhorizon scales. In both cases, the additional corrections induced by the inhomogeneous cutoff cancel the ultraviolet boundary terms arising in the ordinary diagrams. These calculations establish, within cutoff regularization, the late-time constancy of both power spectra and clarify its physical origin. We then investigate the squeezed one-loop scalar bispectrum and show that the additional cutoff contributions are essential for satisfying the consistency relation at finite cutoff. Finally, we discuss the role of the inhomogeneous cutoff in the late-time constancy of the one-loop bispectrum.

conclusions: In an expanding universe with long-wavelength perturbations, keeping the physical ultraviolet cutoff scale $\Lambda_{\rm UV}$ identical across different Hubble patches requires a locally rescaled comoving cutoff: $\Lambda \to a(t)\Lambda_{\rm UV}e^{\zeta_L}[\hat{k}_i\hat{k}_j(e^{-\gamma_L})^{ij}]^{-1/2}$.

Expanding this field-dependent integration boundary in powers of the long-wavelength background generates new regulator-induced loop contributions, which act diagrammatically as soft-mode insertions on regulated loop contractions (such as tadpoles).

For both the one-loop scalar and tensor primordial power spectra, these extra boundary contributions exactly cancel the spurious UV-divergent boundary terms that arise in standard homogeneous cutoff calculations, proving that superhorizon perturbations remain strictly conserved (time-independent) at one loop.

In the squeezed limit of the one-loop scalar bispectrum (where one momentum mode is much smaller than the other two), the inhomogeneous cutoff contributions are essential to ensure that Maldacena's single-field consistency relation holds at finite cutoff.
ai.relevance_reason: Although the paper leverages the separate-universe approximation and studies backreaction of short modes on long-wavelength backgrounds, it is purely focused on quantum loop regularization during early-universe inflation rather than late-time large-scale structure or relativistic N-body cosmology.
ai.summary: When calculating quantum loop corrections to primordial fluctuations during inflation, physicists must introduce a high-energy (ultraviolet, or UV) momentum cutoff to keep the integrals finite. Because long-wavelength perturbations stretch or squeeze the local spatial geometry once they cross outside the causal horizon, a standard uniform comoving cutoff ($a\Lambda_{\rm UV}$) accidentally regulates different causal patches of the universe at different local physical energy scales, breaking general relativistic coordinate invariance. To solve this, the authors apply the "separate universe" picture—treating each horizon-sized patch as a locally homogeneous universe rescaled by the long-wavelength scalar ($\zeta_L$) and tensor ($\gamma_L$) fluctuations—and define an inhomogeneous comoving momentum cutoff that fixes the same physical UV scale for every local observer. Expanding this perturbation-dependent cutoff boundary generates new diagrammatic counterterms that link short-wavelength quantum loops to long-wavelength background modes. The authors demonstrate that these extra boundary terms exactly cancel spurious UV divergences in the one-loop scalar and tensor power spectra and squeezed bispectrum, confirming within cutoff regularization that primordial perturbations freeze out and remain conserved on superhorizon scales.

papers.title: UV Bounds on Inflationary Parity Violation
papers.authors: Alexander Cassem, Mark P. Hertzberg
papers.abstract: A question of fundamental interest is whether parity is violated on large scales in the Universe. This possibility has been motivated by recent analyses of the four-point matter correlation function. It has also been suggested that detectable parity violation could be generated during inflation by the dynamical Chern-Simons operator, a leading effective field theory correction to general relativity. In this work, we examine this possibility in realistic UV completions, including fermionic and string-theoretic examples. We show that existing bounds on the tensor-scalar-scalar (TSS) bispectrum strongly constrain the possibility of generating a detectable parity-odd trispectrum. For tensor-to-scalar ratios near current observational limits, detectability is incompatible with, or pushes against, the regime of validity of these UV completions. A detectable signal can remain possible for a sufficiently small tensor-to-scalar ratio, but only at the cost of an extremely large enhancement of the TSS vertex. Thus, while a future search for large scale parity violation is worth pursuing, generating a detectable signal within a consistent effective theory is highly nontrivial.

conclusions: Current observational bounds on the parity-even tensor-scalar-scalar (TSS) bispectrum already restrict the parity-odd scalar trispectrum amplitude $\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{odd}} = \Pi_{\mathrm{c}} r F$ (where $r$ is the tensor-to-scalar ratio, $F$ is a vertex enhancement factor, and $|\Pi_{\mathrm{c}}| \le 1$ is the fractional chirality of the graviton propagator), leaving little room for a detectable signal when $r$ is near current observational limits.

Requiring a consistent high-energy (UV) completion severely tightens the bound on the graviton chirality parameter from the naive $|\Pi_{\mathrm{c}}| \le 1$ to $|\Pi_{\mathrm{c}}| \ll 5.9 \times 10^{-3}$ in chiral fermion completions, with similarly stringent limits in heterotic and Type IIB string compactifications once perturbativity ($N_7 g_s \lesssim 1$ for $N_7$ D7-branes) and EFT validity are enforced.

Because both $\Pi_{\mathrm{c}}$ and the product $r F$ are tightly bounded, generating a parity-odd trispectrum detectable by upcoming large-scale structure surveys requires an extreme, non-standard enhancement of the TSS vertex $F$ combined with a very small tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$.
ai.relevance_reason: Although motivated by parity-odd 4-point galaxy clustering measurements in large-scale structure, the paper focuses on primordial non-Gaussianity and UV completions of inflationary effective field theories rather than late-time non-linear LSS modelling, beyond-$\Lambda$CDM simulations, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: In an isotropic and homogeneous universe, spatial parity violation (an asymmetry between left- and right-handed spatial configurations) cannot appear in the 2-point power spectrum or 3-point bispectrum of density fluctuations, making the 4-point correlation function (the trispectrum) the lowest-order statistic where it can be detected in galaxy surveys. A popular way to generate such a primordial signal during inflation is through dynamical Chern-Simons (dCS) gravity, an effective field theory (EFT) modification to General Relativity where the rolling inflaton couples to a parity-odd curvature term ($\phi \,{}^*RR$), making graviton exchange chiral (favoring one graviton helicity over the other). The authors investigate whether the dCS coupling can actually be made large enough to produce an observable parity-odd trispectrum without breaking the underlying high-energy (ultraviolet, or UV) physics—testing concrete UV completions involving chiral fermions as well as heterotic and Type IIB string theory—while also satisfying existing observational bounds on the parity-even tensor-scalar-scalar (TSS) bispectrum. They show that keeping the EFT mathematically consistent and within observational bispectrum limits forces the dCS coupling to be very small, meaning that any future detection of large-scale parity violation would be exceedingly difficult to explain with standard dCS inflation unless the graviton-inflaton-inflaton interaction vertex is dramatically enhanced.

papers.title: STEPSIC: Initial condition generator for stereographic cosmological simulations
papers.authors: Balázs Pál, Gábor Rácz, István Csabai, István Szapudi
papers.abstract: We present STEPSIC, an open-source initial condition generator for cosmological N-body simulations in the periodic cuboid, spherical, and cylindrical geometries supported by StePS. It succeeds the earlier StePS initial condition code and extends it to periodic cuboids with arbitrary aspect ratios and cylindrical topologies. Gaussian density fields are generated on a periodic Fourier grid. First- and second-order Lagrangian perturbation theory (LPT) displacements and velocities are interpolated to lattices or relaxed glasses with radially varying particle masses. For spherical and cylindrical domains, an enclosing periodic box supplies the fields, and a multiresolution scheme matches resolved wavelengths to local particle mass. With identical white noise, the periodic calculation agrees with monofonIC to within $0.05\%$ in power spectrum and $0.15\%$ in median particle displacement. On relaxed spherical and cylindrical glasses, comparison with independent sums over retained Fourier modes gives errors consistent with linear interpolation. For an enclosing box of one domain diameter, the root-mean-square relative displacement of two points in the high-resolution region differs from the infinite-Universe value by at most $0.0014\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ out of $0.5\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ at $z=31$, while domain-scale mean-density variance is suppressed. In one cylindrical realization evolved to $z=0$, doubling the enclosing box shifts the high-resolution region by $0.39\,h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$; after removing this bulk displacement, power spectra differ by at most $1.05\%$. In a cylindrical StePS simulation evolved to $z=0$, first-order initial conditions leave up to $3.6\%$ less nonlinear power than second-order ones, consistent with LPT transients.

papers.title: Prospects for multi-messenger discovery of the gravitational-wave background anisotropies via cross-correlation with galaxies
papers.authors: Raphael Bertrand-Delgado, Felipe Andrade-Oliveira, Michael Ebersold, Marcelle Soares-Santos
papers.abstract: We present new empirically grounded forecasts for the observability of stochastic gravitational-wave background anisotropies assuming a population of stellar-mass compact binary coalescences as its source. We quantified the discovery potential using simulations based on the Euclid Flagship Galaxy Catalogue and LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observational constraints in combination with detailed theoretical modelling. We considered the multi-messenger cross-correlation with galaxies as well as the gravitational wave-only cross-correlation across observation-time bins. We found that signal-to-noise ratio greater than five is achievable via cross-correlation of a galaxy catalogue that is complete up to limiting magnitude $i < 24.7$ and has redshift uncertainties $\sigma_z = 0.003 (1+z)$ with a gravitational-wave sky map corresponding to 2 years of observation by a third-generation detector network comprising three interferometers. Network configurations with LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA plus up to two third-generation detectors would be limited to moderate signal-to-noise levels, between three and five, except if merger rates are near the upper bound set by observational constraints, in which case the threshold of five would be reached after 4 years. Detectability without the multi-messenger tracer has proven significantly more challenging, with signal-to-noise ratio remaining below three after 10 years. In light of the plans being carried out in the community for ongoing and upcoming galaxy surveys, this work bodes well for the multi-messenger discovery and exploration of the stochastic gravitational-wave background in the era of next-generation observatories such as the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer.

papers.title: Stochastic constant-roll inflation beyond the hilltop with the spectral method
papers.authors: Eemeli Tomberg
papers.abstract: Stochastic inflation can be used to study large inflationary perturbations. This paper presents such a study for a quadratic hilltop potential, corresponding to constant-roll inflation. I solve the perturbation distribution using the spectral method, with detailed solutions of the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the Fokker-Planck operator. Contrary to previous studies of stochastic constant-roll inflation, the solution allows trajectories that cross the hilltop and get stuck near a reflecting boundary on the other side, tunneling out slowly in a way dictated by the lowest eigensolution. Despite their rarity, these trajectories turn out to dominate the mean first-passage time. For this reason, I argue the mean does not properly describe the inflationary background. Using the median instead, I compute the distribution of the coarse-grained $\Delta N$ distribution and show that its well-known exponential tail first flattens out and then forms a peak near a maximal $\Delta N$ value. I argue similar intricacies arise in primordial black hole models.

papers.title: Direct Primary Beam Correction: A Regularised Linear Operator for Untangling Mutual Coupling in SKA-Low 21-cm Cosmology
papers.authors: Oscar S.D. O'Hara, Quentin Gueuning, Eloy de Lera Acedo, John Cumner, Dominic Anstey, Anthony Brown, Fred Dulwich, Andrew Faulkner, Ashish Mhaske, Oskar Zetterstrom
papers.abstract: Mutual coupling has emerged as the dominant direction-dependent corruption in dense aperture arrays, imprinting spatial and sub-MHz spectral structure that compromises time-gating and foreground-removal strategies. We introduce \textit{direct primary beam correction}, a domain-agnostic, regularised, direction-weighted linear inversion of stacked Jones matrices that transforms an aperture array's far-field pattern towards an arbitrary target. Using full-wave electromagnetic simulations of SKA-Low and a 4-hour observation of the EoR0 field spanning 122--134~MHz, we show that the correction reproduces the target pattern exactly for as many directions as there are elements, with regularisation trading in-field accuracy for sidelobe conditioning. For 21-cm power-spectrum analysis, we introduce a cross-time estimator that correlates samples within each $uv$ cell only between different time blocks. As the field is tracked, sidelobe emission decorrelates between blocks, suppressing its coupling-induced leakage into the EoR window; however, the main beam's coupling-induced chromaticity remains coherent and biases the recovered power, a bias that longer integration does not remove. Combined with the correction, the estimator recovers the input power without bias and passes a foreground-only null test, trading the systematic bias for statistical scatter that averages down over independent correction cycles. Propagating Gaussian beam-model errors shows that detection requires embedded element patterns accurate to at least 3.25 significant figures for channel-independent errors. In contrast, common approximations, such as averaged or neighbouring-channel patterns, reach at most two. Mutual coupling is therefore correctable in principle, making beam characterisation, rather than the correction, the priority for 21-cm experiments with dense aperture arrays.

papers.title: The Goldstone Awakens: Unimodular dark energy in scale-invariant $R^2$ gravity
papers.authors: Mariaveronica De Angelis, Javier Rubio
papers.abstract: We construct an $R^2$ cosmology based on scale invariance and unimodular gravity in which the Goldstone boson of dilatations establishes a predictive connection between inflation and dark energy. The conservation of the corresponding Noether current confines the inflationary trajectory to a one-dimensional orbit in field space, freezing the Goldstone direction and rendering the inflationary dynamics effectively single field. After inflation, the system settles on a Minkowski vacuum manifold. The unimodular integration constant, already present in the full theory but negligible during inflation, lifts the flat Goldstone direction, generating an exponential potential for the canonically normalised field. Unlike in phenomenological quintessence models, its slope is not a free DE parameter, but is instead fixed by the field-space geometry inherited from the inflationary attractor. This geometry excludes matter-era tracking and, throughout the inflationary viability region, places the field in the thawing regime compatible with accelerated expansion. For a representative inflationary benchmark, the now pseudo-Goldstone field remains frozen until close to the present epoch, yielding DE equation-of-state parameters $(w_0,w_a)\simeq(-0.992,-0.011)$ in the CPL parametrisation $w(a)=w_0+w_a(1-a)$. More generally, the same parameter controlling the inflationary spectral tilt also fixes the slope of the DE potential, leading to a tight correlation between early- and late-Universe observables: increasing the thawing signal lowers $n_s$, while values of $n_s$ closer to unity drive the model towards $\Lambda$CDM.

papers.title: Gravitational Waves from Superconducting Cosmic Strings
papers.authors: Jinyoung Jhun, Takashi Hiramatsu
papers.abstract: We study the evolution of superconducting cosmic-string networks in a $U(1)_{\rm local}\times U(1)_{\rm global}$ field-theoretic model using three-dimensional lattice field simulations in an expanding universe. The scalar field charged under $U(1)_{\rm local}$ forms cosmic strings, while the scalar field associated with $U(1)_{\rm global}$ acts as a current carrier and condenses in their vicinity. We investigate the evolution of the string network for several values of the coupling constant between the string-forming and current-carrier fields and estimate the gravitational-wave power spectrum sourced by the resulting superconducting cosmic-string network. We find that the spectral shape depends on the coupling constant: as the interaction strength increases, the spectrum is suppressed on small scales. This feature may be probed by future high-frequency gravitational-wave observations.

papers.title: Black holes from a Higgs-like field in the radiation era
papers.authors: Ethan Milligan, Luis E. Padilla, David J. Mulryne
papers.abstract: Light spectator fields during inflation can acquire superhorizon fluctuations that cross a potential barrier between positive and negative regions of their potential. Motivated by the Standard Model Higgs instability, in this work we study the subsequent evolution of patches where this occurs in the radiation era after inflation ends for a Higgs-like spectator field. We utilise fully nonlinear, spherically symmetric numerical relativity. Across the black hole forming configurations in our investigation we find a robust two-stage evolution. First, the central negative potential region reverses its expansion, becomes kinetic dominated, and forms a primordial black hole that hides the runaway core. The positive potential barrier that survives outside this first horizon then determines one of two late-time branches. In the subcritical branch the original apparent horizon grows smoothly and engulfs the remaining scalar structure. In the supercritical branch, however, the potential energy of the barrier dominates the local evolution. The result is a transient wormhole throat, a bifurcating trapping horizon, and an inflating child universe branch. In both branches the parent radiation dominated universe is ultimately left with an ordinary primordial black hole whose subsequent growth is governed by radiation accretion.

papers.title: Hydrostatic Equilibrium Estimate of the Fuzzy Dark Matter Mass from Dwarf Spheroidals: Method and Systematics
papers.authors: Samrat Mitra, Koushik Dutta
papers.abstract: We present an estimator of an effective fuzzy (wave) dark matter (FDM) boson mass based on local hydrostatic equilibrium, which requires no soliton or other parametric density template. The condition requires the classical gravitational acceleration to be balanced by the gradient of the quantum potential in the Schrödinger--Poisson--Madelung system. We apply it to the density and enclosed-mass posteriors of nine Milky Way dwarf spheroidal (dSph) galaxies obtained with \textsc{pyGravSphere}. For each posterior realization, we determine by least squares the boson mass that best satisfies the force-balance condition over a fixed radial window. This gives a distribution of \(m_{21}\equiv m/10^{-21}\,\mathrm{eV}\) for each galaxy. The per-galaxy median masses range from \(m_{21}\sim 8\) to \(46\), corresponding to \(m\sim(0.8\text{--}4.6)\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{eV}\); Draco and Ursa Minor have the lowest median masses, while Carina and Sextans have the highest. The inverse-variance-weighted effective equilibrium mass of the nine galaxies is \(m=(1.31\pm0.35)\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{eV}\), with Draco and Ursa Minor contributing most of the weight. We also examine the systematic uncertainties in our results.

papers.title: An Empirically Calibrated [C II] Luminosity-Halo Mass Relation for Line Intensity Mapping
papers.authors: Oliver Jeong, Yi-Kuan Chiang, Martin White
papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave line intensity mapping (LIM) aims to observe the high-redshift universe through the 158 $\mu$m fine-structure line of [C II], the brightest far-infrared line of star-forming galaxies. Whether the clustering of large-scale structure, which carries rich cosmological information, is measurable in the [C II] signal at $z>4$ or buried under the shot noise of the emitters is determined from the amplitude and shape of the [C II] power spectrum. We calibrate $L(M_h,z)$ on [C II] data alone: the mean [C II] intensity from tomographic cross-correlation at $0<z<4.2$ and the luminosity-function measurements and limits at $z\simeq0$ and $4.3\lesssim z\lesssim8$. We model the relation as a double power law and fit its four parameters at $z=4.5$ and 5.5 separately, with no assumption about their evolution, and then jointly across $0<z<7$, and we examine how the uncertainty depends on the modeling assumptions. The shape of the power spectrum is settled by the existing data. The clustering peak stands a factor of $45\,(23-93)$ and $64\,(38-112)$ above the shot-noise floor at $z=4.5$ and 5.5, and the two cross at $k_c\simeq 0.37$ and 0.44 $h$ Mpc$^{-1}$. The amplitude is known less well, the clustering power to $0.5-0.6$ dex and the shot noise to $0.7-0.9$ dex. The luminosity-weighted bias, which together with the mean intensity sets the clustering amplitude, is known to about 10\% within the assumptions of this work and is relatively high, about 4. The results show that the signal comes from halos of $10^{11}-10^{12}\,M_\odot$, similar in mass to the hosts of the Lyman-break galaxies and Ly$\alpha$ emitters that galaxy surveys map at these redshifts.

papers.title: BAO and Type Ia Supernovae in LTB Cosmology: Constraints on Radial Inhomogeneity and Acoustic-Ruler Evolution
papers.authors: Myrto Magklara, Leandros Perivolaropoulos
papers.abstract: We investigate how baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) and Type Ia supernovae constrain radial density profiles and acoustic-ruler evolution in Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi (LTB) cosmology with a cosmological constant. A consistent extension of a homogeneous analysis requires modified distances and unequal radial and transverse ruler stretching. Transverse BAO and supernovae isolate ruler evolution without fixing its absolute length. We connect this test to exact nonlinear, compensated density profiles with free depth, width, shell location and exterior matter density, keeping the observer at the symmetry centre. We fit DESI DR2 BAO and DES-Dovekie supernovae with full covariances and matched calibration freedom in LTB and flat $\Lambda$CDM. Conditional on evaluating BAO predictions at effective redshifts, LTB improves the full-sample $\chi^2$ by 8.5 with three additional parameters. DESI rejects the specific deep profile preferred without it, while distinct profiles remain nearly degenerate. Selecting DES supernovae alone gives a shallower shell and a gain of 7.44, almost entirely from BAO and unchanged by an additional magnitude-uncertainty cut. Two illustrative redshift-window tests retain a DES-only gain close to 7 at this geometry. The preferred profile and ruler history depend on the supernova selection. The full-sample gain occurs in at least 7% of simulated flat-$\Lambda$CDM data sets and does not establish an inhomogeneity detection; this calibration is not transferred to DES-only fits. Small finite-ruler corrections do not validate survey-bin averaging. In the local approximation, common LTB ruler evolution shifts angular and transverse three-dimensional BAO together and cannot by itself explain their discrepancy.

papers.abstract: Applications of strong gravitational lensing in astrophysics and cosmology critically depend on building reliable strong lensing models, which require accurate measurements of on-sky positions of multiple images and of the redshifts of the background sources from which they originate. In this context, Euclid is a unique facility, as it simultaneously provides high-resolution multi-band photometric imaging and slitless spectroscopy for an unprecedentedly large sample of gravitational lenses, most of which are newly discovered. In this work, we exploit Euclid slitless spectroscopic data to determine the redshifts of four spatially extended lensed sources, and to reconstruct emission-line images. Specifically, two of the target sources are lensed into giant arcs by the massive galaxy clusters SPT-CLJ0411$-$4819 ($z_\mathrm{d}=0.424$, where "d" denotes the lensing deflector) and Abell 2280 ($z_\mathrm{d}=0.326$). The third system is a quadruply imaged active galactic nucleus (AGN) candidate strongly lensed by a massive galaxy at $z_\mathrm{d}=0.68$, while the fourth is a galaxy-scale Einstein ring produced by a lens galaxy at $z_\mathrm{d}=0.235$. This work represents a proof of concept for the exploitation of Euclid slitless spectroscopic data in the study of strong gravitational lensing, providing one of the first determinations of spectroscopic redshifts for strongly lensed features from NISP spectra. These results demonstrate the feasibility of applying the same methodology to the very large sample of gravitational lenses that Euclid has started to discover and is expected to identify over the course of the mission.

papers.title: Origin of the angular momentum of filaments in the local Universe
papers.authors: V.G. Gurzadyan, N.N. Fimin, V.M. Chechetkin
papers.abstract: Velocity gradients compatible with rotation have been reported across certain nearby cosmic filaments. We show that rotational momentum might be generated in filaments in the local Universe in the presence of a cosmological constant (local dark energy) based on the theorem stating the general function for the equivalence of the gravitational field of a sphere and that of a point mass. We investigated how the cosmological constant modifies the finite-time acquisition and retention of angular momentum in an open filamentary core. Although its isotropic force exerts no direct axial torque, rotational motion can be seeded by tidal interactions with surrounding matter and incoming streams. Early tidal torques establish an imbalance in axial angular momentum, while the subsequent orbit crossing amplifies the resulting rotation, and ultimately, the cosmological constant is able to modify tidal-mode growth and finite-time angular momentum delivery.

papers.title: Two-dimensional Pulsar Distance Inference from Nanohertz Gravitational Waves
papers.authors: Si-Ren Xiao, Ji-Yu Song, Yue Shao, Ling-Feng Wang, Jing-Fei Zhang, Xin Zhang
papers.abstract: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are limited in localizing nanohertz continuous gravitational waves (CGWs) by uncertainties in pulsar distances. We introduce a method to infer pulsar distances in two dimensions, using phase information from the pulsar terms of multiple CGW sources. Our approach can enhance distance precision relative to existing one-dimensional distance-inference methods. Using idealized SKA-motivated PTA simulations with prospective pulsar-distance priors, we combine information from five high-SNR CGW sources with known sky positions and luminosity distances. For example, our method achieves subparsec precision for a simulated pulsar at $0.8\,\mathrm{kpc}$ in $40\%$ of realizations, compared with none for the existing one-dimensional method. Such improvements in pulsar-distance precision could facilitate CGW host-galaxy identification and multimessenger observational prospects.

papers.title: Probing the dynamical inverse seesaw mechanism with low-frequency gravitational waves
papers.authors: Debasish Borah, Sounak Dutta, Partha Kumar Paul, Indrajit Saha, Narendra Sahu
papers.abstract: We study the possibility of probing the dynamical inverse seesaw mechanism for the origin of light neutrino masses via the detection of stochastic gravitational waves (GW) in the low-frequency regime currently being probed by pulsar timing arrays. As the lepton number-violating term in inverse seesaw typically remains in the sub-MeV ballpark, its dynamical origin naturally brings the possibility of a low-scale first-order phase transition, which can be probed at low-frequency GW experiments. We also find interesting complementarity with heavy neutral lepton searches, as GW experiments remain sensitive to parameter space with small active-sterile mixing, which is out of reach for most particle physics experiments.

papers.title: Gravitational Duals from Equations of State II: Large Hierarchies and False Vacua
papers.authors: Raul Jimenez, David Mateos, Pavlos Protopapas, Pau Solé-Vilaró, Pedro Tarancón-Álvarez, Pablo Tejerina-Pérez
papers.abstract: We investigate the reconstruction of holographic duals for strongly coupled quantum field theories in regimes characterized by large hierarchies and the presence of false vacua. Within the gauge/gravity duality, these features translate into non-trivial thermodynamic behaviour and exotic renormalization group flows, including skipping flows between non-adjacent fixed points. Building on previous work based on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), we extend the holographic inverse problem of reconstructing the bulk scalar potential from boundary thermodynamic data into this new regime. This setting presents a variety of conceptual and numerical challenges, such as near-degenerate states, large hierarchies of energy scales, and regions of the potential that are not directly probed by the input data. We develop a set of methodological advances that overcome these obstacles, thereby improving the established PINNs-based methodology and extending it to new physical regimes of interest that were previously out of reach. Applying the developed framework, we demonstrate accurate reconstruction of scalar potentials deep into the false vacuum regime, achieving robust agreement with the physical features of the underlying thermodynamics despite significant numerical stiffness. Our results extend the bridge between holography and machine learning, and suggest that data-driven approaches can provide new insights into the structure of strongly coupled systems.

papers.title: Preheating and oscillon formation in Einstein-scalar-Gauss-Bonnet gravity
papers.authors: Areef Waeming, Josu C. Aurrekoetxea, Katy Clough, Pau Figueras, Áron D. Kovács
papers.abstract: Non-perturbative processes in the early universe may create overdense structures in scalar fields like the inflaton, called oscillons. In this work, we explore whether the leading order higher derivative contributions to the scalar-tensor theory change the formation and growth of these structures, and investigate the limits in which the effective field theory (EFT) description breaks down. We find that whilst the properties of the oscillons are not significantly modified, and black holes do not generically form, for large couplings the period of formation can result in the evolution leaving the regime of validity of the EFT, at which point predictivity is lost and the next order terms in the EFT should become relevant. If the oscillons survive their formation, they tend to be stable and the EFT corrections remain bounded. The EFT breakdown is triggered by large curvature terms in the metric in the densest regions of the oscillon, meaning that approximations of such modified theories that neglect the local backreaction and non-linear dynamics of the fields may miss important effects.

papers.title: Fast Radio Bursts Trace Cosmic Star Formation with Little Delay
papers.authors: Yi-Ying Wang, Yin-Jie Li, Yi-Zhong Fan
papers.abstract: The progenitor channels of fast radio bursts (FRBs) remain debated, with a central question being whether their cosmic rate traces star formation promptly or instead follows it with the long time-delay characteristic of compact-binary mergers. We perform a forward-modeling, hierarchical Bayesian analysis of the CHIME/FRB population, jointly fitting the catalog sample, baseband fluences, and localized host redshifts, while self-consistently incorporating the survey selection function through the injection framework. Adopting the classical cosmic star formation history (SFH) with a range of delay-time models, we find that the reconstructed FRB rate robustly tracks the SFH peak. All models exclude characteristic delays $\Delta t_d > 1.0$ Gyr at the 90\% credible level, with inferred median peak offsets in the range $\Delta t_d = 0.1$--$0.3$ Gyr that remain consistent with a prompt, zero-delay origin at the 2$\sigma$ level. This finding disfavors the previously reported multi-Gyr delays, strongly indicating that the central engine is linked to young remnants (likely magnetars) from stellar collapse and, potentially, to the prompt merger of compact objects.

papers.title: gevolution 2.0: GPU-accelerated relativistic N-body simulations for cosmology
papers.authors: Julian Adamek, Øyvind Christiansen
papers.abstract: High-performance computing is increasingly dominated by hardware acceleration using Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). To take advantage of this long-term trend, we implement a major overhaul of the parallelisation approach in the relativistic particle-mesh N-body code gevolution. The new version 2.0 of gevolution employs three layers of parallelisation: MPI for scalability on a distributed memory system, shared memory parallelisation on each MPI rank using OpenMP, and offloading all compute intensive tasks to GPUs using CUDA. The code also includes many new features that have been developed over the past years. We provide an overview of the code structure and show key performance benchmarks. This publication is accompanied by the simultaneous public release of gevolution 2.0 and of a GPU-ready version of the LATfield2 library which provides the parallelisation backend.

papers.title: Monopoles, Strings, Walls and Gravitational waves
papers.authors: Rinku Maji, Qaisar Shafi
papers.abstract: The gauge symmetry breaking $SU(2) \to U(1) \to Z_2 \to 1$ successively produces monopoles, strings and domain walls bounded by strings (WBS), with the elementary monopole carrying a $U(1)$ magnetic flux twice as large as the elementary string. The elementary strings and subsequently WBS emit gravitational waves, and during their decay, the WBS yield a network of composite strings that carry the same $U(1)$ flux as the monopoles. Depending on the cosmological evolution, we provide the gravitational wave spectra generated by the elementary strings and WBS, in combination with the composite strings which are either effectively stable, quasistable, or metastable. These three scenarios are also realized in the symmetry breaking chain $SU(3) \to SO(3) \to Z_2 \to 1$. Both $SU(2)$ and $SU(3)$ have appeared in the literature as flavor gauge symmetries.

papers.title: FRIDA: Finding Rotation In ultra-Diffuse gAlaxies. I. Programme overview, resolved gas density profiles, and HI mass-size relation
papers.authors: Pavel E. Mancera Piña, Tom Oosterloo, Filippo Fraternali, Elizabeth A. K. Adams, Andrea Afruni, Cecilia Bacchini, Enrico M. Di Teodoro, Lexi Gault, Anastasia A. Ponomareva, Justin I. Read, Barbara Šiljeg
papers.abstract: Gas-rich ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) provide powerful tests of galaxy formation models at low surface densities. However, the structure of their neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) remains poorly constrained, hampering our understanding of this population. We present FRIDA (Finding Rotation In ultra-Diffuse gAlaxies), a MeerKAT and VLA programme providing high-resolution HI data of 12 gas-rich UDGs. In this paper, we introduce our sample and delve into the associated observations and data reduction. We derive HI fluxes, masses ($M_{\rm HI}$), and resolved surface density profiles ($\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)$). We find extended ($\sim 7-30\ \rm{kpc}$ in radius) and regular HI emission in our UDGs, and we report the discovery of a satellite around one of them. Most UDGs in FRIDA have $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)$ profiles with flat inner parts reaching $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)\approx 4\ M_\odot\ \rm{pc^{-2}}$ near their centres, which then decline exponentially in their outer parts. By modelling the HI morphology of the UDGs, we find a median inclination of $43^\circ$, in agreement with theoretical expectations for disc galaxies under UDG selection effects. Moreover, we place our UDGs in the $M_{\rm HI}-R_{\rm HI}$ and $M_{\rm HI}-R_{\rm 50,HI}$ mass-size relations, where $R_{\rm HI}$ is radius at which $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R)=1\ M_\odot \rm{pc^{-2}}$, and $R_{\rm 50,HI}$ is the radius enclosing $50\%$ of $M_{\rm HI}$. While our UDGs lie within the scatter of the relations, they systematically fall on their upper side, being slightly (by $\sim 15-25\%$) more extended and of lower mean $\Sigma_{\rm HI}$ (by $\sim 25-35\%$) than average galaxies at similar $M_{\rm HI}$. Moreover, we find that $\Sigma_{\rm HI}(R/R_{\rm HI})$ and $M_{\rm HI}(<R)/M_{\rm HI}$ for UDGs follow an intermediate trend between late-type discs and early-type galaxies, with a large overlap with Sa galaxies.
